Galactose disorders surface earlier than fructose disorders because of ingestion of breast milk (lactose = galactose + glucose).
Fructose disorders don’t surface until infant commences fruit, juice, honey, and/or table sugar (sucrose = fructose + glucose).
Trapped galactose-1-phosphate in liver sequesters / uses up phosphate.
Worse than galactokinase deficiency.
Should be noted that chloride moves the opposite direction in sweat glands – i.e., rather than CTFR functioning to secrete Cl-, it reabsorbs it, hence our positive sweat chloride test.
The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, K (All Dogs Eat Kittens).
All vitamin D-related endocrine relations are pass-level for the Steps, so know these really well. -
Required for night vision, skin turnover, and immune function.
Topical tretinoin is first-line for acne. It shuts off sebum production and increases epithelial cell turnover.
Oral isotretinoin (high concentration vitamin A) is last-line because of its adverse effects but is most effective for acne.
Both of these treatments cause photosensitivity and desquamation (peeling of skin).

High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic, so must do beta-hCG before starting isotretinoin. Some Qs will also advise commencing birth control before use, or will require educating the patient about barrier contraception, etc.
If USMLE asks most likely teratogenicity in Q about vitamin A, choose cleft lip/palate. Topical tretinoin is not teratogenic.
Vitamin A excess causes cerebral edema with pseudotumor cerebri (i.e., high intracranial pressure, papilledema, confusion), hepatotoxicity (increased liver enzymes), and dyslipidemia.
Isotretinoin and ursine (bear) are the two most common causes of vitamin A toxicity.
Deficiency causes nyctalopia, squamous metaplasia, and immunodeficiency.
Deficiency is rare because Vitamin A is fat-soluble and also stored in high amounts in the liver in Ito cells.
Deficiency caused by malabsorptive disorders - i.e., CF, chronic pancreatitis, Crohn disease.
Vitamin A (all-trans retinoic acid) can be used as treatment for some types of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML).
Tryptophan is a precursor to niacin synthesis. Hartnup disease (↓ ability to reabsorb tryptophan in PCT of kidney) leads to niacin deficiency.
Tryptophan is also precursor to serotonin. Carcinoid syndrome consumes tryptophan, since serotonin is produced, leading to niacin deficiency in some cases.

Deficiency of B3 causes pellagra (dementia, dermatitis, diarrhea). Can present with delirium (biggest risk factor for delirium is underlying dementia). The dermatitis will be either Casal necklace, hyperpigmentation of forearms, or blistering.

B3 excess causes hyperinsulinemia (insulin resistance and diabetes), hyperuricemia (gout), and flushing (due to prostaglandin production, not histamine). Aspirin/NSAIDs can be used to prevent/mitigate flushing, so it makes sense that prostaglandin, not histamine, is the cause.
Q will tell you guy has big cardiovascular history and podagra (gout of big toe; don’t confuse with pellagra) and then ask which agent is contraindicated → answer = niacin (since can cause gout).
Deficiency causes: ↑ homocysteine and no change methylmalonic acid. In B12 deficiency, both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are ↑.

Hypervitaminosis D (vitamin D excess) can occur due to granulomatous diseases. On USMLE this is always sarcoidosis → epithelioid macrophages within non-caseating granulomas produce 1a-hydroxylase without the need for PTH → calcitriol increases → ↑ small bowel absorption of Ca → PTH is suppressed.
For high vitamin D (sarcoidosis), select ↑ Ca, ↑ PO4, ↓PTH.
Williams syndrome → AD, chromosome 7, elfin-like facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia secondary to increased vitamin D sensitivity.
B9 deficiency: normal methylmalonic acid (or methylmalonyl-CoA), ↑ homocysteine.
B12 deficiency: ↑ methylmalonic acid (or methylmalonyl-CoA), ↑ homocysteine.
However B12 alone is needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA.

PWS and AS can also be caused by uniparental disomy, where both alleles are erroneously inherited from the same imprinted parent. § For PWS (maternal uniparental disomy), since the gene is normally maternally imprinted, if both alleles are inherited from mom, both will be silenced; disease occurs because there’s no paternal allele available to be expressed. § For AS (paternal uniparental disomy), since the gene is normally paternally imprinted, if both alleles are inherited from dad, both will be silenced; disease occurs because there’s no maternal allele available to be expressed.

23M + develops pancreatic cancer + mom had colon cancer + uncle had liver cancer; investigative studies show mutation in TP53 gene; Q asks, which process accounts for difference in presentation among family members; answer = pleiotropy; diagnosis is Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 gene mutation results in p53 protein abnormality).

Pleiotropy refers to unrelated phenotypes resulting from a mutation in a single gene. A HY USMLE example is unrelated types of cancers in family members with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is another HY example (i.e., mutation can result in partial albinism and mental retardation, which are unrelated phenotypic traits). Pleiotropy need not refer to different traits phenotypically expressed in the same individual.

Variable expressivity, in contrast, does not specifically refer to the aspect of multiple, disparate phenotypes caused by a single gene, but instead refers to differences in disease severity among individuals with a condition that demonstrates a predictable spectrum of findings. For instance, NF1 is a HY example of a condition with both variable expressivity and pleiotropy. One family member might have more severe disease with café au lait spots, pheochromocytoma, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), whereas another family member has milder disease with only axillary/groin freckling; the difference in disease severity between family members along the predictable spectrum of possible features of NF1 refers to variable expressivity. The pleiotropic aspect refers to mutations in NF1 merely causing different phenotypes, such as pheochromocytoma versus café au lait spots. Conditions that demonstrate variable expressivity must demonstrate complete (100%) penetrance as part of the definition.

Penetrance refers to the percentage of those with a diseased genotype who demonstrate the diseased phenotype to any degree. In other words, if 100% of those with a diseased genotype express the disease phenotypically in some form, then the disease is said to be completely penetrant (NF1 is an example). If the diseased genotype does not result in a disease phenotype in all individuals, then the disease is said to be incompletely penetrant (BRCA1/2 causing breast cancer that “skips a generation” is an example).

hySections.heading: Silent
bullets: Codon sequence is altered at third position, resulting in new codon that codes for the same amino acid – i.e., no change in protein primary sequence.
“Wobble” refers to the mutational “leniency” of this third codon position, where mutation does not cause change in the amino acid coded for.

“Wobble” is nature’s way of striking a balance between potentially advantageous vs deleterious mutations (i.e., allowing just enough mutations to enable evolution but not so much as to permit incessant pathology).

hySections.heading: Splice-site
bullets: The answer if Q mentions a mutation within an intron sequence, or if the Q says an intron was erroneously retained within the final mRNA (i.e., it wasn’t spliced out).
b-thalassemia is HY condition often caused by splice-site mutations in intron sequences.

hySections.heading: Free ribosomes
bullets: Produce proteins that are used intracellularly (i.e., are not exocytosed).

hySections.heading: Golgi
bullets: Processes and packages proteins for modification and exocytosis after receiving them from the RER.

The answer for I-cell disease if they ask for location of the enzyme defect. That is, the patient cannot synthesize mannose-6-phosphate at the Golgi in order to tag lysosomal proteins for trafficking to the lysosomes, so these lysosomal enzymes end up in the plasma instead.

hySections.heading: Mitochondrion
bullets: Site of aerobic respiration (i.e., Kreb cycle + electron transport chain).

Drugs that cause uncoupling/diminution of proton gradient in intermembrane space lead to ↑ ratio of O2 consumed per ATP produced (i.e., ↑ O2 consumption/ATP production ratio → more O2 needed to generate same amount of ATP → heat production).
Mitochondrial disorders present with buzzy triad of 1) ear/eye problems, 2) lactic acidosis, and 3) hypotonia.
Maternally inherited (i.e., males do not transmit disease to offspring).
“Ragged red fibers” is buzzy term for mitochondrial disorder on USMLE.
Heteroplasmy is varying severity of disease in patients with mitochondrial disorders due to differing fractions of diseased mitochondrial genes inherited.
For instance, a child might have decreased hearing and mild hypotonia, whereas his sister has diminished hearing + vision + severe lactic acidosis + severe hypotonia.

Any type of shock on USMLE (i.e., septic, cardiogenic, hypovolemic, etc.) can present with lactic acidosis due to ↓ oxygen delivery to tissues → ↓ ability for mitochondria to conduct aerobic respiration → ↑ anaerobic glycolysis, where pyruvate gets converted to lactate, rather than sent through the TCA cycle.

hySections.heading: Centriole
bullets: Produce mitotic spindles, which are composed of microtubules and form during M-phase of cell cycle (i.e., mitosis).
HY Drugs that inhibit microtubule formation: griseofulvin, mebendazole, colchicine, vincristine, vinblastine.

HY Drugs that inhibit microtubule disassembly: The taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel). These are the odd ones out because they hyperstabilize microtubules / prevent microtubule disassembly. The others prevent microtubule formation.
Griseofulvin → used orally for tinea capitis. Answer on USMLE is “oral griseofulvin for patient only.” Giving to close contacts is wrong answer.
Mebendazole → used for many helminth infections.

hySections.heading: Nucleus
bullets: Eukaryotes only.
Site of DNA replication and transcription to RNA.
Nucleoli are the site within the nucleus where rRNA is synthesized; “prominent nucleoli” in Q means ↑ protein synthesis and ↑ cancer grade (i.e., # of mitoses).
↑ nuclear/cytosplasm ratio (e.g., if Q says it approaches 1:1) indicates high cancer grade – i.e., indicates ↑ mitoses.
Nuclear envelope proteins are phosphorylated during mitosis (ridiculous, but on Step 1 NBME).

hySections.heading: Lysosome
bullets: Contain hydrolytic enzymes for digestive processes.
A phagolysosome refers to when a phagosome (the vesicle that is created during phagocytosis) merges with a lysosome.

Chediak-Higashi syndrome → phagolysosomal fusion disorder characterized by immunodeficiency, partial albinism, and giant granules within phagocytes. Melanosomes require phagolysosome function to be intact, which is why the Q can say the child has lighter skin than a sibling. And the "giant granules" descriptor is buzzy for Chediak-Higashi.
There are many lysosomal storage disorders, which I discuss later.

hySections.heading: Labile
bullets: Remain in G1; never enter G0 (quiescent phase).
HY examples: Gut epithelium, hair follicles, skin, germ cells, bone marrow.
Most affected by chemo-/radiotherapy because of rapid turnover.

hySections.heading: Stable (quiescent)
bullets: Enter G1 from G0 when stimulated.
HY Examples: Hepatocytes, renal tubular cells.
Regeneration of liver → answer = “enter G1 from G0”.
USMLE will mention liver regenerative ability, and then the answer is something like, “reemergence from G0 quiescent phase.”

hySections.heading: Permanent
bullets: Always in G0; regenerate from stem cells.
HY examples: Neurons, cardiac + skeletal muscle cells.
USMLE will tell you someone is exposed to radiation + ask what is most likely to be unaffected, answer is “cardiac myocytes” (the only answer listed that isn’t labile).

hySections.heading: B-48
bullets: Required to move chylomicrons out of the enterocytes into lymphatics/circulation.
Deficient in abetalipoproteinemia (acanthocytes; clear droplets in enterocytes).

hySections.heading: B-100
bullets: Binds to LDL receptor; enables clearance of cholesterol from blood.

hySections.heading: C-II
bullets: Cofactor for lipoprotein lipase (LPL).
Deficient in familial hyperchylomicronemia (or deficiency of LPL).
Fibrates upregulate lipoprotein lipase and Apo-CII and are most effective med for ↓ TGAs.

hySections.heading: Hyperchylomicronemia (AR)
bullets: Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or Apolipoprotein C-II.
↑ chylomicrons + TGAs.
The answer on USMLE if the Q says the plasma appears “creamy.”
Pancreatitis (abdo pain more likely than chest pain) and xanthomas.

hySections.heading: Hypercholesterolemia (AD)
bullets: Deficiency (heterozygous) or absence (homozygous) of LDL receptor or Apo B-100.
↑ LDL. Usually 3-400 in heterozygotes, with MI/death in 30-40s (answer = deficiency of functional LDL receptor).
LDL usually 700-1000 in homozygotes, with MI in teens (answer = absence of functional LDL receptor).
The answer for early death from MI that is familial. Can cause Xanthomas.

hySections.heading: Hypertriglyceridemia (AD)
bullets: ↑ Hepatic production of VLDL.
↑ TGAs on lab report. LDL will be normal.
Pancreatitis.

hySections.heading: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
bullets: Arylsulfatase A — Cerebroside sulfate — - Progressive neurologic decline.

hySections.heading: Krabbe
bullets: Galactocerebrosidase — Galactocerebroside, psychosine — - Aka Globoid cell leukodystrophy. - Globoid cells (giant, multinucleated cells). - Neurodegeneration.

hySections.heading: Fabry (XR)
bullets: a-galactosidase A — Ceramide trihexoside — - Angiokeratomas (small, red/purple dots on the skin due to capillary dilation). - Heart and/or renal problems. - Can cause burning feet/hands (“Fabry crises”).

hySections.heading: Hurler
bullets: a-L-iduronidase — Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) – — - Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. - Yes, clouded corneas. - More severe form of Hunter.

hySections.heading: Hunter (XR)
bullets: Iduronate sulfatase — i.e., Dermatan + heparan sulfates — - Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. - No clouded corneas. - “Hunters can see the X” → Therefore XR and no clouded corneas.

hySections.heading: Galactokinase deficiency
bullets: Deficiency of galactokinase. LOL!
From birth (milk lactose → galactose + glucose); screened via heel-prick test.
Cataracts in neonate. Aldose reductase converts galactose → galactitol, which has ↑↑ osmotic pull in lens, leading to swelling and osmotic damage.
Milder than classic galactosemia.

hySections.heading: Classic galactosemia
bullets: Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.
Cataracts in neonate.
Hepatomegaly, jaundice, hypoglycemia.
Associated with E. coli sepsis.

hySections.heading: Essential fructosuria
bullets: Deficiency of fructokinase.
Benign condition.
Mere presence of “reducing sugars” in the urine.
Negative glucose oxidase urine test (indicating reducing sugars are not glucose).

hySections.heading: Hereditary fructose intolerance
bullets: Deficiency of aldolase B.
Begins with dietary introduction of juice, fruit, honey, and table sugar.
Trapped fructose-1-phosphate in liver sequesters / uses up phosphate.
Worse than essential fructosuria.

hySections.heading: Copper
bullets: Essential cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes crosslinking collagen.

Excess copper seen with Wilson disease → AR, chromosome 13; inability to secrete copper into bile; leads to ↑ copper in urine + ↓ serum ceruloplasmin; causes cirrhosis, Parkinsonism (Cu deposition in basal ganglia, especially the putamen), Kayser-Fleischer rings (deposition in Descemet membrane of cornea); Tx is penicillamine (copper chelator).
Deficiency seen in Menkes disease → XR; inability to absorb Cu in duodenum; causes “wiry” or “springy” hair.

hySections.heading: Iron
bullets: Main use is in hemoglobin. If you didn’t know this basic point, you’re f-u-c-k-e-d-d-d.

Excess seen in hereditary hemochromatosis → AR, chromosome 6; leads to increased duodenal absorption of iron (i.e., cannot shut off absorption); causes Bronze diabetes → hyperpigmentation due to hemosiderin, diabetes due to Fe deposition in tail of pancreas, and various other findings such as arthritis (pseudogout), infertility, and cardiomyopathy; Tx is serial phlebotomy; chelators are the wrong answer in hereditary hemochromatosis; deferoxamine or deferasirox are chelators given in transfusional siderosis (secondary hemochromatosis due to chronic blood transfusions).

hySections.heading: Huntington
bullets: AD; chromosome 4; >40 CAG repeats = disease.
Encodes huntingtin protein (yes, different spelling).
Neurodegeneration with cognitive decline and choreoathetosis beginning in 40s or 50s.
Anticipation is expansion of TNR length with each generation, resulting in earlier and more severe onset of disease.

hySections.heading: Friedreich ataxia
bullets: AR; chromosome 9; GAA expansion.
Encodes frataxin protein.
Ataxia, kyphoscoliosis, cardiomyopathy, pes cavus (high-arched feet), hammer toes, early-onset type II diabetes.

The answer for I-cell disease if they ask for location of the enzyme defect. That is, the patient cannot synthesize mannose-6-phosphate at the Golgi in order to tag lysosomal proteins for trafficking to the lysosomes, so these lysosomal enzymes end up in the plasma instead.
Site of aerobic respiration (i.e., Kreb cycle + electron transport chain).

Drugs that cause uncoupling/diminution of proton gradient in intermembrane space lead to ↑ ratio of O2 consumed per ATP produced (i.e., ↑ O2 consumption/ATP production ratio → more O2 needed to generate same amount of ATP → heat production).
Mitochondrial disorders present with buzzy triad of 1) ear/eye problems, 2) lactic acidosis, and 3) hypotonia.
Maternally inherited (i.e., males do not transmit disease to offspring).
“Ragged red fibers” is buzzy term for mitochondrial disorder on USMLE.
Heteroplasmy is varying severity of disease in patients with mitochondrial disorders due to differing fractions of diseased mitochondrial genes inherited.
For instance, a child might have decreased hearing and mild hypotonia, whereas his sister has diminished hearing + vision + severe lactic acidosis + severe hypotonia.

Any type of shock on USMLE (i.e., septic, cardiogenic, hypovolemic, etc.) can present with lactic acidosis due to ↓ oxygen delivery to tissues → ↓ ability for mitochondria to conduct aerobic respiration → ↑ anaerobic glycolysis, where pyruvate gets converted to lactate, rather than sent through the TCA cycle.
Produce mitotic spindles, which are composed of microtubules and form during M-phase of cell cycle (i.e., mitosis).
HY Drugs that inhibit microtubule formation: griseofulvin, mebendazole, colchicine, vincristine, vinblastine.

HY Drugs that inhibit microtubule disassembly: The taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel). These are the odd ones out because they hyperstabilize microtubules / prevent microtubule disassembly. The others prevent microtubule formation.
Griseofulvin → used orally for tinea capitis. Answer on USMLE is “oral griseofulvin for patient only.” Giving to close contacts is wrong answer.
Mebendazole → used for many helminth infections.
Colchicine → Used for acute gout and pericarditis in patients who can’t receive NSAIDs (i.e., GI bleeds, renal insufficiency, NSAID allergy).
Vincristine → used as chemotherapy; neurotoxic. Q will literally just give you massive paragraph where patient has neuro issues + is on vincristine, and the answer will be “toxic neuropathy.”
Vinblastine → used as chemotherapy.
Taxanes → used as chemo. But just remember these are the odd ones out.
The USMLE can give you one of the above drugs and ask you what they inhibit, and the answer can be just “tubulin.”
Eukaryotes only.
Site of DNA replication and transcription to RNA.
Nucleoli are the site within the nucleus where rRNA is synthesized; “prominent nucleoli” in Q means ↑ protein synthesis and ↑ cancer grade (i.e., # of mitoses).
↑ nuclear/cytosplasm ratio (e.g., if Q says it approaches 1:1) indicates high cancer grade – i.e., indicates ↑ mitoses.
Nuclear envelope proteins are phosphorylated during mitosis (ridiculous, but on Step 1 NBME).
Contain hydrolytic enzymes for digestive processes.
A phagolysosome refers to when a phagosome (the vesicle that is created during phagocytosis) merges with a lysosome.

Chediak-Higashi syndrome → phagolysosomal fusion disorder characterized by immunodeficiency, partial albinism, and giant granules within phagocytes. Melanosomes require phagolysosome function to be intact, which is why the Q can say the child has lighter skin than a sibling. And the "giant granules" descriptor is buzzy for Chediak-Higashi.
There are many lysosomal storage disorders, which I discuss later.
Remain in G1; never enter G0 (quiescent phase).
HY examples: Gut epithelium, hair follicles, skin, germ cells, bone marrow.
Most affected by chemo-/radiotherapy because of rapid turnover.

USMLE will tell you someone is exposed to radiation then ask for what they’re most likely to experience in the next 24 hours → answer = gastrointestinal disturbance, where the other answers listed aren’t labile.
Enter G1 from G0 when stimulated.
HY Examples: Hepatocytes, renal tubular cells.
Regeneration of liver → answer = “enter G1 from G0”.
USMLE will mention liver regenerative ability, and then the answer is something like, “reemergence from G0 quiescent phase.”
Always in G0; regenerate from stem cells.
HY examples: Neurons, cardiac + skeletal muscle cells.
USMLE will tell you someone is exposed to radiation + ask what is most likely to be unaffected, answer is “cardiac myocytes” (the only answer listed that isn’t labile).

19F + eats meal; which of the following molecules is most likely to stimulate glycolysis in this patient; answer = AMP; AMP + ADP stimulate glycolysis; ATP, NADH, citrate, and alanine inhibit glycolysis.

22F + goes for a run; Q asks which enzyme will most likely be activated initially by exercise in this patient; answer = phosphorylase kinase, which will phosphorylate and activate glycogen phosphorylase, the main enzyme that removes glucose-1-phosphate (G1P) units from long glycogen branches and chains. In other words, before glycogen phosphorylase can do its job, it first needs to be phosphorylated and activated by phosphorylase kinase. After the glycogen branch has enough G1P units removed where it is now only four G1P units in length, the first debranching enzyme 1,4- glucosidase removes three of these units, leaving only one left. The second debranching enzyme 1,6- glucosidase removes the final G1P unit.
Required to move chylomicrons out of the enterocytes into lymphatics/circulation.
Deficient in abetalipoproteinemia (acanthocytes; clear droplets in enterocytes).
Binds to LDL receptor; enables clearance of cholesterol from blood.
Cofactor for lipoprotein lipase (LPL).
Deficient in familial hyperchylomicronemia (or deficiency of LPL).
Fibrates upregulate lipoprotein lipase and Apo-CII and are most effective med for ↓ TGAs.
Mediates particle uptake by the liver.
Major protein component of HDL.
Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or Apolipoprotein C-II.
↑ chylomicrons + TGAs.
The answer on USMLE if the Q says the plasma appears “creamy.”
Pancreatitis (abdo pain more likely than chest pain) and xanthomas.
Deficiency (heterozygous) or absence (homozygous) of LDL receptor or Apo B-100.
↑ LDL. Usually 3-400 in heterozygotes, with MI/death in 30-40s (answer = deficiency of functional LDL receptor).
LDL usually 700-1000 in homozygotes, with MI in teens (answer = absence of functional LDL receptor).
The answer for early death from MI that is familial. Can cause Xanthomas.
↑ Hepatic production of VLDL.
↑ TGAs on lab report. LDL will be normal.
Pancreatitis.
Plasmids have three main components: 1) origin of replication (where DNA replication is initiated), 2) polylinker (site where endonucleases act), 3) antibiotic resistance gene.
G-proteins are incredibly annoying concept if you’re seeing this concept for first time, but you need to know three classes for USMLE and how agonism/antagonism causes intracellular changes:

Receptors for G-alpha-s: Beta 1, Beta 2, Dopamine 1, Histamine 2, Vasopressin 2 (essentially memorize both aforementioned mnemonics, and then the receptors that don’t fit into either you know are G-alpha-s). § In other words, for isoproterenol (beta 1 and 2 agonist), the answer is “increased cAMP.” § Likewise, for propranolol (beta 1 and 2 antagonist), the answer is “decreased cAMP.”
Glycogen storage diseases
All autosomal recessive and can present with hepatomegaly. Glycogen storage diseases
Lysosomal storage diseases
All AR except for Fabry and Hunter (XR).
- “Crumpled tissue paper” (lipid-laden) macrophages.
Arylsulfatase A — Cerebroside sulfate — - Progressive neurologic decline.
Galactocerebrosidase — Galactocerebroside, psychosine — - Aka Globoid cell leukodystrophy. - Globoid cells (giant, multinucleated cells). - Neurodegeneration.

a-galactosidase A — Ceramide trihexoside — - Angiokeratomas (small, red/purple dots on the skin due to capillary dilation). - Heart and/or renal problems. - Can cause burning feet/hands (“Fabry crises”).
a-L-iduronidase — Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) – — - Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. - Yes, clouded corneas. - More severe form of Hunter.
Iduronate sulfatase — i.e., Dermatan + heparan sulfates — - Gargoyle-like facies, stridor, aggressive behavior. - No clouded corneas. - “Hunters can see the X” → Therefore XR and no clouded corneas.
Collagen disorders Collagen type Where found Disease(s) HY points
Fractures at different stages of healing.
Often mistaken for child abuse.
Blue sclerae (too easy; often omitted from Qs). I Bone, Late wound healing (white in color), ↑ tensile strength compared to type III. Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)
Conductive hearing loss (malformation of ossicles).

If ruled out OI + child abuse, think osteopetrosis. II Cartilage, Intervertebral discs, vitreous humor. Stickler syndrome - Congenital hearing loss. III Blood vessels, Early wound healing (pink in color) Ehlers-Danlos (vascular type)
Hyperextensible skin/joints. ↓ tensile strength compared to type I.
Easy bruising.
Aortic dissection/regurgitation.
Mitral valve prolapse.
Circle of Willis berry (saccular) aneurysms. IV - Alport (XR; mutation in type IV collagen); eye/ear problems in male with hematuria.
Goodpasture (Abs against type IV collagen); male 20s-40s with hemoptysis + hematuria; linear immunofluorescence pattern on biopsy. Basement membrane (kidney, alveoli). Alport, Goodpasture
Sugar disorders:
Both galactose and fructose disorder vignettes may carry the descriptor of “reducing sugars” in the urine. Galactose disorders are detected by heel prick test at birth.
Galactose disorders surface earlier than fructose disorders because of ingestion of milk (lactose = galactose + glucose).
Fructose disorders don’t surface until infant commences fruit, juice, honey, and/or table sugar (sucrose = fructose + glucose). Sugar disorders for USMLE
Both galactose and fructose disorder vignettes may carry the descriptor of “reducing sugars” in the urine.
Galactose disorders are detected by heel prick test at birth.
Galactose disorders surface earlier than fructose disorders because of ingestion of breast milk (lactose = galactose + glucose).
Fructose disorders don’t surface until infant commences fruit, juice, honey, and/or table sugar (sucrose = fructose + glucose).
Deficiency of galactokinase. LOL!
From birth (milk lactose → galactose + glucose); screened via heel-prick test.
Cataracts in neonate. Aldose reductase converts galactose → galactitol, which has ↑↑ osmotic pull in lens, leading to swelling and osmotic damage.
Milder than classic galactosemia.
Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.
Cataracts in neonate.
Hepatomegaly, jaundice, hypoglycemia.
Associated with E. coli sepsis.
Trapped galactose-1-phosphate in liver sequesters / uses up phosphate.
Worse than galactokinase deficiency.
Deficiency of fructokinase.
Benign condition.
Mere presence of “reducing sugars” in the urine.
Negative glucose oxidase urine test (indicating reducing sugars are not glucose).
Deficiency of aldolase B.
Begins with dietary introduction of juice, fruit, honey, and table sugar.
Trapped fructose-1-phosphate in liver sequesters / uses up phosphate.
Worse than essential fructosuria.
Should be noted that chloride moves the opposite direction in sweat glands – i.e., rather than CTFR functioning to secrete Cl-, it reabsorbs it, hence our positive sweat chloride test.
The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, K (All Dogs Eat Kittens).
All vitamin D-related endocrine relations are pass-level for the Steps, so know these really well. -
Required for night vision, skin turnover, and immune function.
Topical tretinoin is first-line for acne. It shuts off sebum production and increases epithelial cell turnover.
Oral isotretinoin (high concentration vitamin A) is last-line because of its adverse effects but is most effective for acne.
Both of these treatments cause photosensitivity and desquamation (peeling of skin).

High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic, so must do beta-hCG before starting isotretinoin. Some Qs will also advise commencing birth control before use, or will require educating the patient about barrier contraception, etc.
If USMLE asks most likely teratogenicity in Q about vitamin A, choose cleft lip/palate. Topical tretinoin is not teratogenic.
Vitamin A excess causes cerebral edema with pseudotumor cerebri (i.e., high intracranial pressure, papilledema, confusion), hepatotoxicity (increased liver enzymes), and dyslipidemia.
Isotretinoin and ursine (bear) are the two most common causes of vitamin A toxicity.
Deficiency causes nyctalopia, squamous metaplasia, and immunodeficiency.
Deficiency is rare because Vitamin A is fat-soluble and also stored in high amounts in the liver in Ito cells.
Deficiency caused by malabsorptive disorders - i.e., CF, chronic pancreatitis, Crohn disease.
Vitamin A (all-trans retinoic acid) can be used as treatment for some types of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML).
Tryptophan is a precursor to niacin synthesis. Hartnup disease (↓ ability to reabsorb tryptophan in PCT of kidney) leads to niacin deficiency.
Tryptophan is also precursor to serotonin. Carcinoid syndrome consumes tryptophan, since serotonin is produced, leading to niacin deficiency in some cases.

Deficiency of B3 causes pellagra (dementia, dermatitis, diarrhea). Can present with delirium (biggest risk factor for delirium is underlying dementia). The dermatitis will be either Casal necklace, hyperpigmentation of forearms, or blistering.

B3 excess causes hyperinsulinemia (insulin resistance and diabetes), hyperuricemia (gout), and flushing (due to prostaglandin production, not histamine). Aspirin/NSAIDs can be used to prevent/mitigate flushing, so it makes sense that prostaglandin, not histamine, is the cause.
Q will tell you guy has big cardiovascular history and podagra (gout of big toe; don’t confuse with pellagra) and then ask which agent is contraindicated → answer = niacin (since can cause gout).
Deficiency causes: ↑ homocysteine and no change methylmalonic acid. In B12 deficiency, both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are ↑.

Hypervitaminosis D (vitamin D excess) can occur due to granulomatous diseases. On USMLE this is always sarcoidosis → epithelioid macrophages within non-caseating granulomas produce 1a-hydroxylase without the need for PTH → calcitriol increases → ↑ small bowel absorption of Ca → PTH is suppressed.
For high vitamin D (sarcoidosis), select ↑ Ca, ↑ PO4, ↓PTH.
Williams syndrome → AD, chromosome 7, elfin-like facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia secondary to increased vitamin D sensitivity.
Essential cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes crosslinking collagen.

Excess copper seen with Wilson disease → AR, chromosome 13; inability to secrete copper into bile; leads to ↑ copper in urine + ↓ serum ceruloplasmin; causes cirrhosis, Parkinsonism (Cu deposition in basal ganglia, especially the putamen), Kayser-Fleischer rings (deposition in Descemet membrane of cornea); Tx is penicillamine (copper chelator).
Deficiency seen in Menkes disease → XR; inability to absorb Cu in duodenum; causes “wiry” or “springy” hair.
Main use is in hemoglobin. If you didn’t know this basic point, you’re f-u-c-k-e-d-d-d.

Excess seen in hereditary hemochromatosis → AR, chromosome 6; leads to increased duodenal absorption of iron (i.e., cannot shut off absorption); causes Bronze diabetes → hyperpigmentation due to hemosiderin, diabetes due to Fe deposition in tail of pancreas, and various other findings such as arthritis (pseudogout), infertility, and cardiomyopathy; Tx is serial phlebotomy; chelators are the wrong answer in hereditary hemochromatosis; deferoxamine or deferasirox are chelators given in transfusional siderosis (secondary hemochromatosis due to chronic blood transfusions).
B9 deficiency: normal methylmalonic acid (or methylmalonyl-CoA), ↑ homocysteine.
B12 deficiency: ↑ methylmalonic acid (or methylmalonyl-CoA), ↑ homocysteine.
However B12 alone is needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA.

PWS and AS can also be caused by uniparental disomy, where both alleles are erroneously inherited from the same imprinted parent. § For PWS (maternal uniparental disomy), since the gene is normally maternally imprinted, if both alleles are inherited from mom, both will be silenced; disease occurs because there’s no paternal allele available to be expressed. § For AS (paternal uniparental disomy), since the gene is normally paternally imprinted, if both alleles are inherited from dad, both will be silenced; disease occurs because there’s no maternal allele available to be expressed.

23M + develops pancreatic cancer + mom had colon cancer + uncle had liver cancer; investigative studies show mutation in TP53 gene; Q asks, which process accounts for difference in presentation among family members; answer = pleiotropy; diagnosis is Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 gene mutation results in p53 protein abnormality).

Pleiotropy refers to unrelated phenotypes resulting from a mutation in a single gene. A HY USMLE example is unrelated types of cancers in family members with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is another HY example (i.e., mutation can result in partial albinism and mental retardation, which are unrelated phenotypic traits). Pleiotropy need not refer to different traits phenotypically expressed in the same individual.

Variable expressivity, in contrast, does not specifically refer to the aspect of multiple, disparate phenotypes caused by a single gene, but instead refers to differences in disease severity among individuals with a condition that demonstrates a predictable spectrum of findings. For instance, NF1 is a HY example of a condition with both variable expressivity and pleiotropy. One family member might have more severe disease with café au lait spots, pheochromocytoma, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), whereas another family member has milder disease with only axillary/groin freckling; the difference in disease severity between family members along the predictable spectrum of possible features of NF1 refers to variable expressivity. The pleiotropic aspect refers to mutations in NF1 merely causing different phenotypes, such as pheochromocytoma versus café au lait spots. Conditions that demonstrate variable expressivity must demonstrate complete (100%) penetrance as part of the definition.

Penetrance refers to the percentage of those with a diseased genotype who demonstrate the diseased phenotype to any degree. In other words, if 100% of those with a diseased genotype express the disease phenotypically in some form, then the disease is said to be completely penetrant (NF1 is an example). If the diseased genotype does not result in a disease phenotype in all individuals, then the disease is said to be incompletely penetrant (BRCA1/2 causing breast cancer that “skips a generation” is an example).
AD; chromosome 4; >40 CAG repeats = disease.
Encodes huntingtin protein (yes, different spelling).
Neurodegeneration with cognitive decline and choreoathetosis beginning in 40s or 50s.
Anticipation is expansion of TNR length with each generation, resulting in earlier and more severe onset of disease.
AR; chromosome 9; GAA expansion.
Encodes frataxin protein.
Ataxia, kyphoscoliosis, cardiomyopathy, pes cavus (high-arched feet), hammer toes, early-onset type II diabetes.

topics.title: Serum biochemistry HY points:
topics.summary: Calcium:

bullets: Calcium:
Normal range: 8.4-10.2 mg/dL.
Low calcium causes “up” presentations - i.e., tetany and hyperreflexia. It can cause long QT on ECG.
High calcium causes “down” presentations of muscle flaccidity and hyporeflexia. It also is associated with delirium/confusion (hypercalcemic crisis) and short QT on ECG.

High calcium HY causes: § Sarcoidosis --> due to high vitamin D. § Primary hyperparathyroidism --> adenoma, hyperplasia, or MEN 1/2A. § Metastatic malignancy --> mets cause cytokine effects at bone, leading to lytic lesions and calcium leaching out of bone. § Multiple myeloma --> lytic lesions. § Thiazides --> cause increased calcium reabsorption in DCT.

Low calcium HY causes: § Rickets/osteomalacia --> deficiency of vitamin D --> decreased small bowel Ca absorption. § Secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure) --> decreased synthesis of 1,25-D3 --> decreased small bowel absorption. § Post-thyroidectomy --> causes concomitant loss of parathyroids --> less calcium resorbed from bone + less 1,25-D3 synthesized in the kidney. § DiGeorge syndrome --> agenesis of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches --> agenesis of parathyroid glands. § Loop diuretics --> cause decreased paracellular Ca reabsorption. § Hypomagnesemia --> causes hypocalcemia and hypokalemia non-responsive to supplementation; usually seen in alcoholics.
Sodium:
Normal range: 135-145 mEq/L.
Sodium derangement (high and low) causes CNS dysfunction --> confusion, stupor, or coma.

Correcting high sodium too quickly with hypotonic saline can cause cerebral edema. Correcting low sodium too quickly with hypertonic saline can cause central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination).

High sodium HY causes: § Primary hyperaldosteronism --> aldosterone pulls sodium out of the urine at the cortical collecting duct. § Renal artery stenosis and fibromuscular dysplasia --> RAAS is increased --> higher aldosterone. § Dehydration --> hemoconcentration of sodium. RAAS would also be increased. § Diabetes insipidus --> cannot reabsorb free water at medullary collecting duct --> serum concentrates as a result.

Low sodium HY causes: § Addison disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome --> aldosterone is low. § Psychogenic polydipsia --> dilutional hyponatremia from excessive water consumption. § DKA --> dilutional hyponatremia from high glucose in the blood --> water stays with glucose. § SIADH --> reabsorbing too much free water at the medullary collecting duct --> serum dilutes.
Potassium:
Normal range: 3.5-5.0 mEq/L.
Potassium derangement (both high and low) causes arrhythmia and muscle weakness.
Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves on ECG. For hyperkalemia with ECG changes, give IV calcium to stabilize the myocardium.
Hypokalemia can cause U waves or flattened T waves on ECG.

High potassium HY causes: § Addison disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome --> aldosterone is low, so less K+ is secreted. § Renal failure --> K+ can't be filtered sufficiently at the glomerulus + cannot be secreted distally sufficiently under the action of aldosterone. § DKA --> insulin isn't present to push potassium into cells + "cellular shift" occurs, where cells take on more H+ from ketoacids, so they kick out K+ to balance charge. It should be noted, however, that low total body potassium occurs in DKA, despite high serum potassium (hyperkalemia). In other words, there is low intracellular K+, but high serum K+. Overall, total body K+ is low. § Polypharmacy with agents such as potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterine) and digoxin. § Congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Low potassium HY causes: § Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome and hyperplasia). § Renal artery stenosis + fibromuscular dysplasia --> high aldosterone. § Cushing disease (chronically high glucocorticoid levels can cause hypo-K due to distal renal secretion similar to mineralocorticoids). § Vomiting + diarrhea --> cause volume depletion --> RAAS increases --> aldosterone kicks out K+. There is also direct loss from GI contents. § Eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia), even if there isn’t purging. Most common cause of death in these disorders is low potassium leading to arrhythmia. § Low total body potassium occurs in DKA, despite high serum potassium (hyperkalemia). § Loop diuretics --> direct loss due to Na/K/2Cl ATPase blockade + indirect loss from volume depletion that leads to increased RAAS. § Thiazides --> cause volume depletion --> increased RAAS. § Hypomagnesemia --> hypomagnesemia can cause hypokalemia and hypocalcemia non-responsive to supplementation; usually seen in alcoholics due to dietary deficiency. Mg is required for PTH release from the parathyroid glands. Mg is also required to prevent renal potassium wasting.
Phosphate:
Normal range: 3-4.5 mg/dL.

High phosphorus HY causes: § Hypoparathyroidism --> kidney retains phosphate at the PCT, since PTH normally causes PO4 loss. § Secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure) --> kidney cannot filter/excrete enough PO4. § Tumor lysis syndrome --> cells release lots of PO4 into blood + acute kidney failure can occur, resulting in high PO4 by extension. § Sarcoidosis --> high 1,25-D3 causes increased small bowel absorption of phosphate (and calcium).

Low phosphorus HY causes: § Primary hyperparathyroidism --> increased phosphate loss at the PCT of the kidney. § Rickets/osteomalacia --> low vitamin D means less absorption of PO4 from small bowel. It should be noted, however, that if the osteomalacia is specifically due to renal failure, then phosphate is still up, since the effect of the renal failure "wins" over the low vitamin D effect. § Refeeding syndrome --> phosphate is consumed by the abrupt increase in glycolytic intermediates requiring phosphate.
Magnesium:
Normal range: 1.7-2.2 mg/dL.

Magnesium derangement causes effects similar to calcium – i.e., low Mg presents with an “up” state of hyperreflexia and increased muscle tone; high Mg presents with a “down” state of hyporeflexia and muscle flaccidity.
Low Mg HY cause is alcoholism (decreased dietary intake) --> leads to hypocalcemia and hypokalemia non-response to supplementation.
High Mg doesn't really exist on USMLE.
HY Acid-base concepts for USMLE:
Normal serum pH: 7.35-7.45.
Normal serum bicarb (HCO3-): 22-28 mEq/L.
Normal arterial pCO2: 33-44 mmHg.
If the Q gives you a respiratory disturbance of any kind, look at pCO2 first in the labs.
If the Q doesn't give you a respiratory disturbance, then the cause of the acid/base disturbance is metabolic, so look at HCO3 first.
CO2 is acidic, so if we're not breathing and it builds up, we get a respiratory acidosis. Likewise, if we blow it off, we'll have respiratory alkalosis (because we're getting rid of an acid).
Bicarb is basic, so if it builds up, we get a metabolic alkalosis. If bicarb is low, we have a metabolic acidosis.
If pH is low:
High CO2 + normal HCO3 = acute respiratory acidosis.
High CO2 + high HCO3 = chronic respiratory acidosis (aka, respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation).
Low HCO3 + low CO2 = acute or chronic metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

Primary metabolic acid/base derangements are compensated for instantly by changes in respiration (i.e., it’s easy to retain or breathe off CO2 merely by changing respiratory rate), whereas primary respiratory derangements are compensated for slowly because it takes time for the kidney to alter bicarb excretion.

Therefore, if CO2 is up or down as the primary issue, a normal HCO3 tells you the problem is acute (i.e., usually within the first day). If bicarb is not in the normal range, then it tells you the issue is chronic.
If pH is high:
Low CO2 + normal HCO3 = acute respiratory alkalosis.
Low CO2 + low HCO3 = chronic respiratory alkalosis (aka, respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation).
High HCO3 + high CO2 = acute or chronic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.
Metabolic acidosis:
Low pH caused by low HCO3; pCO2 will instantly go down to compensate (CO2 is acidic) by merely breathing more.

MUDPILES is mnemonic for high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: § Methanol, Uremia (renal failure). DKA. Propylene glycol / Paracetamol. Iron tablets + Isoniazid. Lactic acidosis. Ethylene glycol (antifreeze). Salicylates (aspirin).
If the patient has metabolic acidosis and the anion gap is normal in the Q, you can eliminate the MUDPILES answers and choose an answer like renal tubular acidosis.
Aspirin is special in that it causes a mixed metabolic acidosis / respiratory alkalosis.
Renal tubular acidosis, Addison, and diarrhea are HY for normal anion gap.
Anion gap is calculated as Na - (HCO3 + Cl). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L. High is 13 or greater.
Metabolic alkalosis:
High pH caused by high HCO3; pCO2 will instantly go up to compensate (CO2 is acidic) by merely breathing less. HY causes are:
Conn syndrome --> aldosterone-secreting tumor means more protons are secreted distally at the cortical collecting duct in the kidney.
Renal artery stenosis + fibromuscular dysplasia --> RAAS is up so aldosterone is up.
Vomiting --> loss of protons in vomitus + volume depletion results in increased RAAS, further kicking out protons distally in the kidney.

Loops and thiazides --> cause "contraction alkalosis," which means volume depletion that causes RAAS to increase --> aldosterone goes up --> more protons secreted distally in the kidney --> metabolic alkalosis.
Respiratory acidosis:
Low pH caused by high CO2; HCO3 goes up only if chronic to compensate (bicarb is basic). It takes time for the kidneys to retain bicarb, so for the first 12-24 hours, bicarb will be normal.

Acute (normal bicarb) HY examples: § Hypoventilation due to opioids, benzos, barbiturates. § Can also be ventilatory insufficiency due to insufficient ventilator settings, or decompensation while on a ventilator.

Chronic (high bicarb) HY examples: § COPD --> these patients are chronic CO2 retainers. Should be noted that exacerbations of COPD are acute on chronic respiratory acidosis, where CO2 will be super high, with the bicarb already high. § § Obstructive sleep apnea / obesity hypoventilation syndrome --> chronic CO2 retainers. § Ankylosing spondylitis + severe kyphoscoliosis --> lesser chest wall expansion.
Respiratory alkalosis:
High pH caused by low CO2; HCO3 goes down only if chronic to compensate (bicarb is basic). It takes time for the kidneys to excrete bicarb, so the first 12-24 hours, bicarb will be normal.

Acute (normal bicarb) HY examples: § Asthma attack --> CO2 is low, not high. This is really HY for USMLE. CO2 only normalizes or goes up if the patient gets tired, which is a danger scenario usually requiring intubuation. § Panic attack --> patient is hyperventilating. § Most pulmonary emboli --> patient is hyperventilating. A low pH in the setting of PE can be seen in Qs, but this is due to lactic acidosis secondary to an obstructive shock process, not the PE directly. § Altitude sickness (first day at high altitude) --> patient is hyperventilating.
Chronic (low bicarb) HY examples: § Living at high altitude; pregnancy (progesterone upregulates respiratory centers).
Winter's formula:
Winter formula is used to calculate predicted pCO2 based on any change in bicarb, where:
Predicted pCO2 = (1.5 x HCO3) + 8 +/- 2.
For example, if a patient has DKA and bicarb is 14 mEq/L, we expect pCO2 to be 27-31 mmHg (1.5 x 14 = 21; 21 + 8 = 29; 29 +/2 = 27-31).
If pCO2 is lower than 27, then the patient has a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.
If pCO2 is higher than 31, then the patient has a concurrent respiratory acidosis.

This type of Q can occasionally show up on USMLE, where if pCO2 is in the expected range, the Q can write the answer as "compensated metabolic acidosis/alkalosis." If the change in CO2 is less than what we expect, the Q can write the answer as "uncompensated metabolic acidosis/alkalosis."
Catecholamine synthesis:
Catecholamines are products derived from tyrosine that can act as both a hormone and a neurotransmitter. The adrenal medulla and CNS neurons are the two locations these are produced.
Phenylalanine --> tyrosine:

Phenylalanine hydroxylase (or THB) is deficient in phenylketonuria (PKU). This is tested for via heelprick test at birth because not catching the disorder can cause mental retardation. Children with PKU present with partial albinism, mousy/musty body odor, and cognitive disability. The Q can say the child is fairer skinned than their sibling. Treatment is special diet without phenylalanine, since buildup of this amino acid causes symptoms. Tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid for the patient since they cannot synthesize it.
Tyrosine --> L-DOPA:

Classic Parkinson disease is not due to deficiency of tyrosine hydroxylase, but instead due to loss of dopamine-secreting neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta of the midbrain. But this enzyme deficiency can very rarely be a cause of Parkinsonism.

Do not confuse tyrosine hydroxylase with tyrosinase. The latter is a HY cause of albinism (oculocutaneous albinism type I). You don't need to memorize this specific albinism type name, but you must know that albinism is often due to enzyme deficiency in general, where the patient cannot synthesize melanin. Tyrosinase converts tyrosine --> DOPA (not L-DOPA) --> dopaquinone in melanin synthesis. The USMLE can give you a vignette of albinism, and then the answer is just simply "enzyme deficiency," or "tyrosinase deficiency." The caveat, however, is that there is an NBME question floating around with a kid with red hair and partial albinism, where tyrosinase deficiency is wrong, but they show you a flow chart of chemical substrates, where it's obvious based on the info they give you that tyrosinase is wrong for that Q. There are numerous types of albinism with different enzyme deficiencies. USMLE probably made this Q so that you don't blanket-memorize tyrosinase deficiency as a 100% cause.
L-DOPA --> Dopamine:

L-Dopa decarboxylase is vitamin B6-dependent. This isn't dramatic if you remember that decarboxylase enzymes are often B6-dependent. Similar to tyrosine hydroxylase, deficiency of L- DOPA decarboxylase can result in dopamine deficiency and Parkinsonism.

Patients with Parkinson disease aren't given dopamine directly, since dopamine has cardiovascular effects. So they are given L-DOPA/Carbidopa. For USMLE, they want you to know this combo "increases BBB penetration of L-DOPA." This is because enzymes that act on L-DOPA will act on carbidopa instead. The term "competitive inhibitor" isn't traditionally applied to carbidopa, but its presence increases the survival of L-DOPA so that it can cross the BBB.
Dopamine --> norepinephrine:

Requires dopamine beta-hydroxylase. For USMLE, you need to know this is vitamin C-dependent. There is NBME Q where they tell you patient has a buildup of dopamine and low NE, and the answer is simply "deficiency of dopamine beta-hydroxylase." Very easy question, but it exists.
Norepinephrine --> epinephrine:

The adrenal medulla is special in that it can convert NE --> E via an enzyme called phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT). You actually do need to know the name of this enzyme for USMLE. This enzyme is upregulated by cortisol. Cortisol diffuses from the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex down to the medulla, where it upregulates PNMT synthesis.

USMLE might tell you a patient's serum ratio of E:NE is 80:20 and ask why, and the answer is just simply "phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase," or "stimulation of epinephrine production by cortisol." The conversion of NE --> adds a methyl group, as implied by the enzyme name. You also need to know this.

The difference between norepinephrine and epinephrine is that E can agonize beta-2 receptors, whereas NE cannot. This means if we block alpha-1 receptors with, e.g,. phentolamine, and then give epinephrine, the beta-2 agonism results in peripheral vasodilation and a drop in blood pressure. This effect does not occur with norepinephrine. You need to know beta-2 agonism causes peripheral dilation and alpha-1 agonism causes peripheral vasoconstriction.

NE and E are high in pheochromocytoma, where a patient will present with paroxysmal (episodic) hypertension, palpitations, and pounding headaches. The patient can sometimes have a BP of 120/80, and then when stressed (e.g., when sitting up on the operating table), have a BP that shoots up to 200/110. Pheochromocytoma can occur idiopathically, or be part of syndromes like NF1 or MEN2A/2B. Treatment is phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha-1 blocker. Do not give a beta- blocker first for treatment, as this will kill the patient. If we block beta receptors first, then we cause "unopposed alpha" binding, where the high amounts of NE and E floating around will bind to alpha-1, causing lots of arteriolar constriction, shooting BP higher and killing the patient.
Alkaptonuria:

Deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase, leading to inability to breakdown both phenylalanine and tyrosine. This will cause blue/black discoloration of cartilage (ochronosis) and arthritis. The USMLE can tell you a patient has ochronosis and urine that turns black with time, or with the addition of citrate. Alkaptonuria is fairly obscure and isn't "HY" per se. But it's pass-level if it shows up because the presentation is so hyper-buzzy on the exam.
Phakomatoses:
Mutation causes constitutive activation of hypoxia-inducible factor.

Investigator looking at cellular effects of increased serum insulin; which of the following combinations of findings is most likely; answer = ↑ nuclear/cytoplasmic shuttling; ↑ serine phosphorylation; ↓ ubiquitination; insulin activates MAP tyrosine kinase and serine/threonine pathways, which will cause ↑ nuclear/cytoplasmic shuttling and ↑ serine phosphorylation; ubiquitination is ↓ because this is a catabolic process but insulin is anabolic.
20M + weakness + twitching + muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibers; Q asks which cellular organelle on the following diagram is impaired.
Answer = mitochondrion; “ragged red fibers” is buzzy description seen in myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF syndrome).
Neonate born with holoprosencephaly + cleft lip; Q asks about chromosomal abnormality; answer = trisomy of chromosome 13; Dx is Patau syndrome.

Neonate + high serum BUN + normal creatinine; a defect in ammoniagenesis; Q asks, which substrate is the most likely source of the ammonia; answer = glutamine; ammonia is produced from the breakdown of various amino acids with amino group side-chains; the ammonia is processed via the urea cycle into urea, which is much less toxic.
Neonate + poor feeding + lethargy + vomiting + increased serum orotic acid + hyperammonemia; which enzyme is deficient; answer = ornithine transcarbamylase.

Experiment is performed analyzed nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kB); Q asks about role of IkB in relation to NF-kB; answer = “releases NF-kB after undergoing phosphorylation”; outrageously dumb and pedantic, but it’s on the NBME so just memorize it.

24F + lost in wilderness for three weeks; Q asks how adipocytes play an important role in maintaining homeostasis; answer = “glucagon activates hormone-sensitive lipase”; HSL will liberate fatty acids from the adipocytes into the blood to be used as energy. Insulin does the opposite by activating lipoprotein lipase; this brings fatty acids from the blood into the adipocytes.

17F + asks about breastfeeding and immunity for her baby; physician explains IgA moves through epithelial cells and is secreted into duct lumina; Q asks which process is best described here; answer = transcytosis, which is movement of substrates from outside one side of the cell, through the interior of the cell, and then out the other side of the cell; this is in contrast to exocytosis, which is merely secreting substrates from inside the cell to the outside; endocytosis is a broad term referring to the internalization of substrates from outside the cell to within; phagocytosis is the engulfment of solid particles; pinocytosis is the engulfment of liquid.

3F + tonic-clonic seizure; Q asks, the Tx for this condition mediates its effect via which type of molecular target; answer = “ligand-gated ion channels”; benzos, e.g., diazepam, are used first-line for status epilepticus; they agonize GABAA, which causes chloride to enter the neuron, hyperpolarizing it. GABA is normally the ligand that binds to its receptor, activating the chloride channel.

42M + 7-month-Hx of shortness of breath on exertion + ejection fraction of 70% + Hx of epistaxis since adolescence + patient’s tongue and finger are shown; Q asks, what is cause of patient’s presentation?

Answer = “pulmonary arteriovenous shunting”; Dx is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu); autosomal dominant; can cause GI bleeding (iron deficiency anemia; fatigue); Q will either show you a red dot on the tongue or finger (telangiectasia); can lead to high-output cardiac failure (EF >70%) in middle age due to AV shunting (as with this patient); vignette can also be pediatric.

Graph Q where the more protein A is bound to a plate, the less protein B is able to bind to the plate; Q asks why this is the case; answer = proteins A and B express the same epitope; epitope = part of an antigen that antibody attaches itself to; don’t confuse with antibody idiotype (Fab) and isotype (Fc), which I talk about in detail in HY Immuno.

34F + breast cancer + BRCA mutation; Q asks what kind of DNA repair is impaired; answer = recombinational dsDNA break repair. In contrast, mismatch repair is answer for Lynch syndrome (HNPCC); nucleotide excision repair is xeroderma pigmentosum.

Q shows you absurdly long sequence of DNA base pairs; exons are bolded; introns are un-bolded; mutation is shown within an un-bolded region (i.e., an intron); Q asks what effect this would most likely have; answer = disruption of normal splicing; mutations within introns are sometimes splice-site mutations; for USMLE, just think: introns = do not become protein + mutations are often splice-site.
Q asks about molecular effect of oxytocin; answer = increases phosphoinositide hydrolysis; oxytocin is G-alpha-q G-protein, which increases IP3 (via hydrolysis of PIP2) and DAG.

Q asks which of the following analyses can help determine monoclonality of neoplastic cells; answer = X-chromosome-linked isoenzymes; isoenzymes are enzymes with different amino acid sequences that catalyze the same chemical reaction; monoclonality refers to a cancer originating from one cell; investigation of G6PD X-linked isoenzymes is a known method for determining clonality of cell populations. Weird and obscure, I get it. But it’s on the NBME.

Bacterial strain produces a mutated protein that functions better at higher temperature; what kind of mutation accounts for this change in function; answer = missense mutation; polymorphisms resulting in differing function are usually missense – i.e., one amino acid is substituted for another.

Q mentions experiment involving abnormal elastin in lab animals; which amino acid is most likely to be abnormal in these lab animals; answer = lysine (need to know elastin contains lots of lysine). Student says, “um ok...” I agree, dumb and pedantic, but it’s on NBME.

12M + cystic fibrosis + ataxia + bilateral diminished reflexes + weakness of lower extremities; which vitamin is deficient (B12 not listed); answer = vitamin E; CF leads to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption; vitamin E deficiency can present with neuropathy; other vitamin deficiencies causing neuropathy: B6 (answer for isoniazid use); B12 (pernicious anemia, chronic gastritis, gastrectomy, terminal ileectomy, Crohn disease, vegetarian/veganism, Diphyllobothrium latum infection); B1 (dry beriberi).

24M + high serum glucose + necrolytic migratory erythema; Q asks which process is most likely upregulated in this patient; answer = oxidation of fatty acids; glucagonoma will force patient into catabolic state (i.e., decreasing relative amount of insulin); in contrast, quick review of some HY wrong answers:

Guy starving in wilderness for three weeks + has decreased muscle mass; which of the following best explains his current status; answer = negative nitrogen balance; this means intake of nitrogen compounds (i.e., protein) is less than utilization by the body, leading to loss of muscle mass; in bodybuilding, a positive nitrogen balance ensures muscle growth.

Q asks for important effect of niacin on patient with increased serum TGAs; answer = antagonizes hepatic VLDL-cholesterol secretion (i.e., decreases TGAs); niacin notably increases HDL (not listed as an answer for this Q + the Q asks about a patient who specifically has high TGAs); PPAR-alpha agonism refers to fibrates (upregulate lipoprotein lipase).

4M + recurrent pancreatitis + high serum cholesterol and TGAs + receives an injection of heparin and this restores his serum lipoprotein lipase activity; which of the following is decreased in this patient; answer = ApoC-II; familial hyperchylomicronemia.
Q asks about cellular effect of Diphtheria toxin; answer = disrupts translation; inhibits elongation factor 2; (same as Pseudomonas).
Q asks about where the receptor for signal-recognition particles is located; answer = RER.
Q asks about which amino acid is necessary in a healthy child’s diet in order to maintain proper nutrition; answer = methionine (essential amino acid); essential amino acid; memorize for USMLE.
Two different Qs asking about G-proteins; first asks effect of albuterol; other asks effect of ranitidine;
Administration of hypotonic saline: ↑ ECF volume; ↓ ECF osmolality; ↑ ICF volume; ↓ ICF osmolality.
Administration of isotonic saline: ↑ ECF volume; no change ECF osmolality; no change ICF volume; no change ICF osmolality.

Patient has peripheral neuropathy + normal MCV + decreased hemoglobin + increased LDH; Q asks for vitamin deficiency (B12 and E both listed); answer = vitamin E deficiency. Increased serum LDH can be seen with hemolysis / RBC turnover; vitamin E deficiency can lead to RBC fragility and hemolysis. B12 deficiency causes increase in MCV.

You can see the entrance of galactose into glycolytic intermediates (i.e., G6P) is closer in proximity to glucose, so there must be a defect between DHAP and G6P in the aforementioned patient. HY BIOCHEMISTRY

hySections.heading: Neurofibromatosis type I (NF1)
bullets: NF1 gene; AD; chromosome 17.
Neurofibromas, café au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), pheochromocytoma, optic nerve glioma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma.

hySections.heading: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC)
bullets: TSC1/2 genes; autosomal dominant.

Periventricular nodules (tubers) on MRI of head, seizures, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypopigmented macules (“ashleaf spots”), hyperpigmented velvety lesions (“shagreen patches”).

hySections.heading: Von Hippel-Lindau
bullets: VHL gene; AD; chromosome 3.
Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas, bilateral renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts.

hySections.heading: Sturge-Weber
bullets: Somatic mosaicism condition; not inherited.
Port wine stain birth mark (nevus flammeus; may also present as violaceous papules in temporal distribution), leptomeningeal angioma (presenting as seizure); glaucoma

hySections.heading: ELISA
bullets: Detects presence of antigen (direct ELISA) or antibody (indirect ELISA) in patient sample.

hySections.heading: PCR
bullets: Amplifies DNA fragments in order to make many copies.

hyBullets: Calcium:
Normal range: 8.4-10.2 mg/dL.
Low calcium causes “up” presentations - i.e., tetany and hyperreflexia. It can cause long QT on ECG.
High calcium causes “down” presentations of muscle flaccidity and hyporeflexia. It also is associated with delirium/confusion (hypercalcemic crisis) and short QT on ECG.

High calcium HY causes: § Sarcoidosis --> due to high vitamin D. § Primary hyperparathyroidism --> adenoma, hyperplasia, or MEN 1/2A. § Metastatic malignancy --> mets cause cytokine effects at bone, leading to lytic lesions and calcium leaching out of bone. § Multiple myeloma --> lytic lesions. § Thiazides --> cause increased calcium reabsorption in DCT.

Low calcium HY causes: § Rickets/osteomalacia --> deficiency of vitamin D --> decreased small bowel Ca absorption. § Secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure) --> decreased synthesis of 1,25-D3 --> decreased small bowel absorption. § Post-thyroidectomy --> causes concomitant loss of parathyroids --> less calcium resorbed from bone + less 1,25-D3 synthesized in the kidney. § DiGeorge syndrome --> agenesis of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches --> agenesis of parathyroid glands. § Loop diuretics --> cause decreased paracellular Ca reabsorption. § Hypomagnesemia --> causes hypocalcemia and hypokalemia non-responsive to supplementation; usually seen in alcoholics.
Sodium:
Normal range: 135-145 mEq/L.
Sodium derangement (high and low) causes CNS dysfunction --> confusion, stupor, or coma.

Correcting high sodium too quickly with hypotonic saline can cause cerebral edema. Correcting low sodium too quickly with hypertonic saline can cause central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination).

High sodium HY causes: § Primary hyperaldosteronism --> aldosterone pulls sodium out of the urine at the cortical collecting duct. § Renal artery stenosis and fibromuscular dysplasia --> RAAS is increased --> higher aldosterone. § Dehydration --> hemoconcentration of sodium. RAAS would also be increased. § Diabetes insipidus --> cannot reabsorb free water at medullary collecting duct --> serum concentrates as a result.

Low sodium HY causes: § Addison disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome --> aldosterone is low. § Psychogenic polydipsia --> dilutional hyponatremia from excessive water consumption. § DKA --> dilutional hyponatremia from high glucose in the blood --> water stays with glucose. § SIADH --> reabsorbing too much free water at the medullary collecting duct --> serum dilutes.
Potassium:
Normal range: 3.5-5.0 mEq/L.
Potassium derangement (both high and low) causes arrhythmia and muscle weakness.
Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves on ECG. For hyperkalemia with ECG changes, give IV calcium to stabilize the myocardium.
Hypokalemia can cause U waves or flattened T waves on ECG.

High potassium HY causes: § Addison disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome --> aldosterone is low, so less K+ is secreted. § Renal failure --> K+ can't be filtered sufficiently at the glomerulus + cannot be secreted distally sufficiently under the action of aldosterone. § DKA --> insulin isn't present to push potassium into cells + "cellular shift" occurs, where cells take on more H+ from ketoacids, so they kick out K+ to balance charge. It should be noted, however, that low total body potassium occurs in DKA, despite high serum potassium (hyperkalemia). In other words, there is low intracellular K+, but high serum K+. Overall, total body K+ is low. § Polypharmacy with agents such as potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterine) and digoxin. § Congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Low potassium HY causes: § Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome and hyperplasia). § Renal artery stenosis + fibromuscular dysplasia --> high aldosterone. § Cushing disease (chronically high glucocorticoid levels can cause hypo-K due to distal renal secretion similar to mineralocorticoids). § Vomiting + diarrhea --> cause volume depletion --> RAAS increases --> aldosterone kicks out K+. There is also direct loss from GI contents. § Eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia), even if there isn’t purging. Most common cause of death in these disorders is low potassium leading to arrhythmia. § Low total body potassium occurs in DKA, despite high serum potassium (hyperkalemia). § Loop diuretics --> direct loss due to Na/K/2Cl ATPase blockade + indirect loss from volume depletion that leads to increased RAAS. § Thiazides --> cause volume depletion --> increased RAAS. § Hypomagnesemia --> hypomagnesemia can cause hypokalemia and hypocalcemia non-responsive to supplementation; usually seen in alcoholics due to dietary deficiency. Mg is required for PTH release from the parathyroid glands. Mg is also required to prevent renal potassium wasting.
Phosphate:
Normal range: 3-4.5 mg/dL.

High phosphorus HY causes: § Hypoparathyroidism --> kidney retains phosphate at the PCT, since PTH normally causes PO4 loss. § Secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure) --> kidney cannot filter/excrete enough PO4. § Tumor lysis syndrome --> cells release lots of PO4 into blood + acute kidney failure can occur, resulting in high PO4 by extension. § Sarcoidosis --> high 1,25-D3 causes increased small bowel absorption of phosphate (and calcium).

Low phosphorus HY causes: § Primary hyperparathyroidism --> increased phosphate loss at the PCT of the kidney. § Rickets/osteomalacia --> low vitamin D means less absorption of PO4 from small bowel. It should be noted, however, that if the osteomalacia is specifically due to renal failure, then phosphate is still up, since the effect of the renal failure "wins" over the low vitamin D effect. § Refeeding syndrome --> phosphate is consumed by the abrupt increase in glycolytic intermediates requiring phosphate.
Magnesium:
Normal range: 1.7-2.2 mg/dL.

Magnesium derangement causes effects similar to calcium – i.e., low Mg presents with an “up” state of hyperreflexia and increased muscle tone; high Mg presents with a “down” state of hyporeflexia and muscle flaccidity.
Low Mg HY cause is alcoholism (decreased dietary intake) --> leads to hypocalcemia and hypokalemia non-response to supplementation.
High Mg doesn't really exist on USMLE.
HY Acid-base concepts for USMLE:
Normal serum pH: 7.35-7.45.
Normal serum bicarb (HCO3-): 22-28 mEq/L.
Normal arterial pCO2: 33-44 mmHg.
If the Q gives you a respiratory disturbance of any kind, look at pCO2 first in the labs.
If the Q doesn't give you a respiratory disturbance, then the cause of the acid/base disturbance is metabolic, so look at HCO3 first.
CO2 is acidic, so if we're not breathing and it builds up, we get a respiratory acidosis. Likewise, if we blow it off, we'll have respiratory alkalosis (because we're getting rid of an acid).
Bicarb is basic, so if it builds up, we get a metabolic alkalosis. If bicarb is low, we have a metabolic acidosis.
If pH is low:
High CO2 + normal HCO3 = acute respiratory acidosis.
High CO2 + high HCO3 = chronic respiratory acidosis (aka, respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation).
Low HCO3 + low CO2 = acute or chronic metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

Primary metabolic acid/base derangements are compensated for instantly by changes in respiration (i.e., it’s easy to retain or breathe off CO2 merely by changing respiratory rate), whereas primary respiratory derangements are compensated for slowly because it takes time for the kidney to alter bicarb excretion.

Therefore, if CO2 is up or down as the primary issue, a normal HCO3 tells you the problem is acute (i.e., usually within the first day). If bicarb is not in the normal range, then it tells you the issue is chronic.
If pH is high:
Low CO2 + normal HCO3 = acute respiratory alkalosis.
Low CO2 + low HCO3 = chronic respiratory alkalosis (aka, respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation).
High HCO3 + high CO2 = acute or chronic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.
Metabolic acidosis:
Low pH caused by low HCO3; pCO2 will instantly go down to compensate (CO2 is acidic) by merely breathing more.

MUDPILES is mnemonic for high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: § Methanol, Uremia (renal failure). DKA. Propylene glycol / Paracetamol. Iron tablets + Isoniazid. Lactic acidosis. Ethylene glycol (antifreeze). Salicylates (aspirin).
If the patient has metabolic acidosis and the anion gap is normal in the Q, you can eliminate the MUDPILES answers and choose an answer like renal tubular acidosis.
Aspirin is special in that it causes a mixed metabolic acidosis / respiratory alkalosis.
Renal tubular acidosis, Addison, and diarrhea are HY for normal anion gap.
Anion gap is calculated as Na - (HCO3 + Cl). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L. High is 13 or greater.
Metabolic alkalosis:
High pH caused by high HCO3; pCO2 will instantly go up to compensate (CO2 is acidic) by merely breathing less. HY causes are:
Conn syndrome --> aldosterone-secreting tumor means more protons are secreted distally at the cortical collecting duct in the kidney.
Renal artery stenosis + fibromuscular dysplasia --> RAAS is up so aldosterone is up.
Vomiting --> loss of protons in vomitus + volume depletion results in increased RAAS, further kicking out protons distally in the kidney.

Loops and thiazides --> cause "contraction alkalosis," which means volume depletion that causes RAAS to increase --> aldosterone goes up --> more protons secreted distally in the kidney --> metabolic alkalosis.
Respiratory acidosis:
Low pH caused by high CO2; HCO3 goes up only if chronic to compensate (bicarb is basic). It takes time for the kidneys to retain bicarb, so for the first 12-24 hours, bicarb will be normal.

Acute (normal bicarb) HY examples: § Hypoventilation due to opioids, benzos, barbiturates. § Can also be ventilatory insufficiency due to insufficient ventilator settings, or decompensation while on a ventilator.

Chronic (high bicarb) HY examples: § COPD --> these patients are chronic CO2 retainers. Should be noted that exacerbations of COPD are acute on chronic respiratory acidosis, where CO2 will be super high, with the bicarb already high. § § Obstructive sleep apnea / obesity hypoventilation syndrome --> chronic CO2 retainers. § Ankylosing spondylitis + severe kyphoscoliosis --> lesser chest wall expansion.
Respiratory alkalosis:
High pH caused by low CO2; HCO3 goes down only if chronic to compensate (bicarb is basic). It takes time for the kidneys to excrete bicarb, so the first 12-24 hours, bicarb will be normal.

Acute (normal bicarb) HY examples: § Asthma attack --> CO2 is low, not high. This is really HY for USMLE. CO2 only normalizes or goes up if the patient gets tired, which is a danger scenario usually requiring intubuation. § Panic attack --> patient is hyperventilating. § Most pulmonary emboli --> patient is hyperventilating. A low pH in the setting of PE can be seen in Qs, but this is due to lactic acidosis secondary to an obstructive shock process, not the PE directly. § Altitude sickness (first day at high altitude) --> patient is hyperventilating.
Chronic (low bicarb) HY examples: § Living at high altitude; pregnancy (progesterone upregulates respiratory centers).
Winter's formula:
Winter formula is used to calculate predicted pCO2 based on any change in bicarb, where:
Predicted pCO2 = (1.5 x HCO3) + 8 +/- 2.
For example, if a patient has DKA and bicarb is 14 mEq/L, we expect pCO2 to be 27-31 mmHg (1.5 x 14 = 21; 21 + 8 = 29; 29 +/2 = 27-31).
If pCO2 is lower than 27, then the patient has a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.
If pCO2 is higher than 31, then the patient has a concurrent respiratory acidosis.

This type of Q can occasionally show up on USMLE, where if pCO2 is in the expected range, the Q can write the answer as "compensated metabolic acidosis/alkalosis." If the change in CO2 is less than what we expect, the Q can write the answer as "uncompensated metabolic acidosis/alkalosis."
