This effect does not occur with norepinephrine. You need to know beta-2 agonism causes peripheral dilation and alpha-1 agonism causes peripheral vasoconstriction.

NE and E are high in pheochromocytoma, where a patient will present with paroxysmal (episodic) hypertension, palpitations, and pounding headaches. The patient can sometimes have a BP of 120/80, and then when stressed (e.g., when sitting up on the operating table), have a BP that shoots up to 200/110. Pheochromocytoma can occur idiopathically, or be part of syndromes like NF1 or MEN2A/2B. Treatment is phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha-1 blocker. Do not give a beta- blocker first for treatment, as this will kill the patient. If we block beta receptors first, then we cause "unopposed alpha" binding, where the high amounts of NE and E floating around will bind to alpha-1, causing lots of arteriolar constriction, shooting BP higher and killing the patient.
Alkaptonuria:

Deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase, leading to inability to breakdown both phenylalanine and tyrosine. This will cause blue/black discoloration of cartilage (ochronosis) and arthritis. The USMLE can tell you a patient has ochronosis and urine that turns black with time, or with the addition of citrate. Alkaptonuria is fairly obscure and isn't "HY" per se. But it's pass-level if it shows up because the presentation is so hyper-buzzy on the exam.
Phakomatoses:
NF1 gene; AD; chromosome 17.
Neurofibromas, café au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), axillary/groin freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), pheochromocytoma, optic nerve glioma, oligodendroglioma, ependymoma.
TSC1/2 genes; autosomal dominant.

Periventricular nodules (tubers) on MRI of head, seizures, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypopigmented macules (“ashleaf spots”), hyperpigmented velvety lesions (“shagreen patches”).
VHL gene; AD; chromosome 3.
Cerebellar/retinal hemangioblastomas, bilateral renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts.
Mutation causes constitutive activation of hypoxia-inducible factor.
Somatic mosaicism condition; not inherited.
Port wine stain birth mark (nevus flammeus; may also present as violaceous papules in temporal distribution), leptomeningeal angioma (presenting as seizure); glaucoma
Detects presence of antigen (direct ELISA) or antibody (indirect ELISA) in patient sample.
Amplifies DNA fragments in order to make many copies.

Investigator looking at cellular effects of increased serum insulin; which of the following combinations of findings is most likely; answer = ↑ nuclear/cytoplasmic shuttling; ↑ serine phosphorylation; ↓ ubiquitination; insulin activates MAP tyrosine kinase and serine/threonine pathways, which will cause ↑ nuclear/cytoplasmic shuttling and ↑ serine phosphorylation; ubiquitination is ↓ because this is a catabolic process but insulin is anabolic.
20M + weakness + twitching + muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibers; Q asks which cellular organelle on the following diagram is impaired.
Answer = mitochondrion; “ragged red fibers” is buzzy description seen in myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF syndrome).
Neonate born with holoprosencephaly + cleft lip; Q asks about chromosomal abnormality; answer = trisomy of chromosome 13; Dx is Patau syndrome.

Neonate + high serum BUN + normal creatinine; a defect in ammoniagenesis; Q asks, which substrate is the most likely source of the ammonia; answer = glutamine; ammonia is produced from the breakdown of various amino acids with amino group side-chains; the ammonia is processed via the urea cycle into urea, which is much less toxic.
Neonate + poor feeding + lethargy + vomiting + increased serum orotic acid + hyperammonemia; which enzyme is deficient; answer = ornithine transcarbamylase.

Experiment is performed analyzed nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kB); Q asks about role of IkB in relation to NF-kB; answer = “releases NF-kB after undergoing phosphorylation”; outrageously dumb and pedantic, but it’s on the NBME so just memorize it.

24F + lost in wilderness for three weeks; Q asks how adipocytes play an important role in maintaining homeostasis; answer = “glucagon activates hormone-sensitive lipase”; HSL will liberate fatty acids from the adipocytes into the blood to be used as energy. Insulin does the opposite by activating lipoprotein lipase; this brings fatty acids from the blood into the adipocytes.

17F + asks about breastfeeding and immunity for her baby; physician explains IgA moves through epithelial cells and is secreted into duct lumina; Q asks which process is best described here; answer = transcytosis, which is movement of substrates from outside one side of the cell, through the interior of the cell, and then out the other side of the cell; this is in contrast to exocytosis, which is merely secreting substrates from inside the cell to the outside; endocytosis is a broad term referring to the internalization of substrates from outside the cell to within; phagocytosis is the engulfment of solid particles; pinocytosis is the engulfment of liquid.

3F + tonic-clonic seizure; Q asks, the Tx for this condition mediates its effect via which type of molecular target; answer = “ligand-gated ion channels”; benzos, e.g., diazepam, are used first-line for status epilepticus; they agonize GABAA, which causes chloride to enter the neuron, hyperpolarizing it. GABA is normally the ligand that binds to its receptor, activating the chloride channel.

42M + 7-month-Hx of shortness of breath on exertion + ejection fraction of 70% + Hx of epistaxis since adolescence + patient’s tongue and finger are shown; Q asks, what is cause of patient’s presentation?

Answer = “pulmonary arteriovenous shunting”; Dx is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu); autosomal dominant; can cause GI bleeding (iron deficiency anemia; fatigue); Q will either show you a red dot on the tongue or finger (telangiectasia); can lead to high-output cardiac failure (EF >70%) in middle age due to AV shunting (as with this patient); vignette can also be pediatric.

Graph Q where the more protein A is bound to a plate, the less protein B is able to bind to the plate; Q asks why this is the case; answer = proteins A and B express the same epitope; epitope = part of an antigen that antibody attaches itself to; don’t confuse with antibody idiotype (Fab) and isotype (Fc), which I talk about in detail in HY Immuno.

34F + breast cancer + BRCA mutation; Q asks what kind of DNA repair is impaired; answer = recombinational dsDNA break repair. In contrast, mismatch repair is answer for Lynch syndrome (HNPCC); nucleotide excision repair is xeroderma pigmentosum.

Q shows you absurdly long sequence of DNA base pairs; exons are bolded; introns are un-bolded; mutation is shown within an un-bolded region (i.e., an intron); Q asks what effect this would most likely have; answer = disruption of normal splicing; mutations within introns are sometimes splice-site mutations; for USMLE, just think: introns = do not become protein + mutations are often splice-site.
Q asks about molecular effect of oxytocin; answer = increases phosphoinositide hydrolysis; oxytocin is G-alpha-q G-protein, which increases IP3 (via hydrolysis of PIP2) and DAG.

Q asks which of the following analyses can help determine monoclonality of neoplastic cells; answer = X-chromosome-linked isoenzymes; isoenzymes are enzymes with different amino acid sequences that catalyze the same chemical reaction; monoclonality refers to a cancer originating from one cell; investigation of G6PD X-linked isoenzymes is a known method for determining clonality of cell populations. Weird and obscure, I get it. But it’s on the NBME.

Bacterial strain produces a mutated protein that functions better at higher temperature; what kind of mutation accounts for this change in function; answer = missense mutation; polymorphisms resulting in differing function are usually missense – i.e., one amino acid is substituted for another.

Q mentions experiment involving abnormal elastin in lab animals; which amino acid is most likely to be abnormal in these lab animals; answer = lysine (need to know elastin contains lots of lysine). Student says, “um ok...” I agree, dumb and pedantic, but it’s on NBME.

12M + cystic fibrosis + ataxia + bilateral diminished reflexes + weakness of lower extremities; which vitamin is deficient (B12 not listed); answer = vitamin E; CF leads to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption; vitamin E deficiency can present with neuropathy; other vitamin deficiencies causing neuropathy: B6 (answer for isoniazid use); B12 (pernicious anemia, chronic gastritis, gastrectomy, terminal ileectomy, Crohn disease, vegetarian/veganism, Diphyllobothrium latum infection); B1 (dry beriberi).

24M + high serum glucose + necrolytic migratory erythema; Q asks which process is most likely upregulated in this patient; answer = oxidation of fatty acids; glucagonoma will force patient into catabolic state (i.e., decreasing relative amount of insulin); in contrast, quick review of some HY wrong answers:

Guy starving in wilderness for three weeks + has decreased muscle mass; which of the following best explains his current status; answer = negative nitrogen balance; this means intake of nitrogen compounds (i.e., protein) is less than utilization by the body, leading to loss of muscle mass; in bodybuilding, a positive nitrogen balance ensures muscle growth.

Q asks for important effect of niacin on patient with increased serum TGAs; answer = antagonizes hepatic VLDL-cholesterol secretion (i.e., decreases TGAs); niacin notably increases HDL (not listed as an answer for this Q + the Q asks about a patient who specifically has high TGAs); PPAR-alpha agonism refers to fibrates (upregulate lipoprotein lipase).

4M + recurrent pancreatitis + high serum cholesterol and TGAs + receives an injection of heparin and this restores his serum lipoprotein lipase activity; which of the following is decreased in this patient; answer = ApoC-II; familial hyperchylomicronemia.
Q asks about cellular effect of Diphtheria toxin; answer = disrupts translation; inhibits elongation factor 2; (same as Pseudomonas).
Q asks about where the receptor for signal-recognition particles is located; answer = RER.
Q asks about which amino acid is necessary in a healthy child’s diet in order to maintain proper nutrition; answer = methionine (essential amino acid); essential amino acid; memorize for USMLE.
Two different Qs asking about G-proteins; first asks effect of albuterol; other asks effect of ranitidine;
Administration of hypotonic saline: ↑ ECF volume; ↓ ECF osmolality; ↑ ICF volume; ↓ ICF osmolality.
Administration of isotonic saline: ↑ ECF volume; no change ECF osmolality; no change ICF volume; no change ICF osmolality.

Patient has peripheral neuropathy + normal MCV + decreased hemoglobin + increased LDH; Q asks for vitamin deficiency (B12 and E both listed); answer = vitamin E deficiency. Increased serum LDH can be seen with hemolysis / RBC turnover; vitamin E deficiency can lead to RBC fragility and hemolysis. B12 deficiency causes increase in MCV.

You can see the entrance of galactose into glycolytic intermediates (i.e., G6P) is closer in proximity to glucose, so there must be a defect between DHAP and G6P in the aforementioned patient. HY BIOCHEMISTRY

bullets: Q asks about which of the following is most likely to disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; answer = “appreciable rate of gene mutation”; H-W assumes: there is no appreciable rate of gene mutation; mating within a population occurs at random; the population is relatively large; there is no selection against a particular genotype; and there is no significant immigrant population.

rapidFireQAs.q: 50F + renal insufficiency due to granulomatosis with polyangiitis. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3, fecal Ca2+ , and 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3, ↑ fecal Ca2+ , ↓ 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — In the PCT of the kidney, we normally have inactive 25-OH-D3 → active 1,25-(OH)2-D3 via 1a- hydroxylase under the action of PTH. • In renal insufficiency, this process is disrupted, so 1,25-D3 levels decrease, and 25-D3 levels rise. • If we are forced to choose an arrow for inactive 25-D3, it would be ↑, since it is not converted sufficiently to 1,25-D3, however, 25-D3 can be converted to another inactive storage form called 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. • For all intents and purposes, on USMLE, think of 24,25-D3 and 25-D3 as the same. If 25-D3 builds up, then so does 24,25-D3. • The caveat is: 24,25-D3 is not converted directly to 1,25-D3. Only 25-D3 is converted to 1,25-D3. • Since active 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3 causes absorption of calcium in the small bowel, if there is reduced 1,25-D3 synthesis, then less calcium is absorbed, and more ends up in the feces. USMLE asks this variable on some of the retired Step 1 NBMEs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 9M + alopecia + determined to have rare condition characterized by an inactivating mutation in his vitamin D receptors. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for serum Ca2+, PTH, and 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Serum Ca2+ , ↑ PTH, ↓ 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — The Step 1 NBME wants you to know the findings for vitamin D receptor insensitivity. • Since vitamin D causes intestinal absorption of calcium, serum calcium will be low. The low calcium causes PTH to go up (due to decreased negative feedback). • The NBME doesn’t ask about phosphate levels for this condition, possibly because whilst vitamin D deficiency will ordinarily cause low phosphate (due to decreased intestinal absorption), it is possible that in patients with chronically elevated PTH in the setting of a vitamin D receptor mutation, phosphate might be variable. • Recall that inactive 25-OH-D3 can be converted to another inactive storage form called 24,25-D3. If PTH is high, then 1a-hydroxylase activity is high, so there will be less 25-D3 available to be shunted to 24,25-D3. The NBME mentions 24,25-D3 levels as “undetectable” in the setting of vitamin D receptor mutation. This also means if USMLE asks you for merely the 25-OH-D3 levels, choose a down arrow. • The NBME gives normal serum levels for 1,25-(OH)2-D3. This might sound weird, since if there’s a mutation in the vitamin D receptor, then theoretically more 1,25-D3 should be produced to compensate. This explains the low 24-25-D3, but perhaps in patients with this condition, 1,25-D3 is often normal, rather than elevated.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + construction worker + chronic alcoholic + consumes lots of fish and milk. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for hepatic hydroxylase activity, renal hydroxylase activity, 25-(OH)-vitamin D3, and 1,25- (OH)2-vitamin D3?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ hepatic hydroxylase activity, ↑ renal hydroxylase activity, ↓ 25-(OH)-D3, ↓ 1,25-(OH)2-D3. — Adequate sunlight means this patient can initiate vitamin D synthesis in the skin without a problem. • Since he is an alcoholic, he will have ↓ hepatic hydroxylase activity and ↓ synthesis of 25-OH-D3. • Since 25-D3 is low, 1,25-D3 will also be low, since there is less substrate to be converted to product. • Low 1,25-D3 means ↓ intestinal absorption of calcium. Even though his diet is rich in calcium, he will not be able to absorb it adequately. PTH will then go up to compensate (less negative feedback). • High PTH will ↑ activity of renal 1a-hydroxylase in an attempt to produce more 1,25-D3. However, the latter is still low because, as we said, 25-D3 is low due to the alcoholism. • USMLE will sometimes give a calcium/vitamin D-type Q with an alcoholic, and the answer will simply be “decreased hepatic hydroxylase activity.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + born at home + bleeding from umbilical stump. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for bleeding time, PT, and aPTT?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Bleeding time, ↑ PT, ↑ aPTT. — Diagnosis is vitamin K deficiency. Bleeding from the umbilical stump in a neonate is the most common presentation for it on Step. • Vignette can also be patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics for many weeks (kills off gut flora that synthesize vitamin K). • Vitamin K activates clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X (and anti-clotting proteins C and S). • Since many clotting factors are impaired, we have high PT and aPTT. • Since platelets are completely normal / are unaffected, bleeding time is normal. Clotting factors have nothing to do with bleeding time.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + eats large turkey dinner. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for activity of glycogen phosphorylase, glucokinase, phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) carboxykinase, and pyruvate carboxylase?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Glycogen phosphorylase, ↑ glucokinase, ↓ PEP carboxykinase, ↓ pyruvate carboxylase. — If you immediately are freaking out about biochemistry stuff, don’t. I don’t want you to obsess over the pathways, etc. As long as you memorize the arrows I write out, you’re good. You can know nothing otherwise. Just know the arrows. → “Michael, that sounds great.” “I know.” • The first thing we have to ask is: is he in the fed or fasting state → he’s in the fed state. • Then we ask, “Ok, well do we expect each enzyme to be active or inactive in the fed state?” • Glycogen phosphorylase breaks down glycogen. Glycogen synthase builds it up. In the fed state, we’d have glycogenesis, not glycogenolysis, so glycogen phosphorylase would be decreased in activity. • Glucokinase is the hexokinase variant in the liver. This is the first enzyme of glycolysis. In the fed state, we have increased glycolysis, so glucokinase is up. • PEP carboxykinase is a gluconeogenic enzyme that converts oxaloacetate to PEP, so that PEP can make its way back up to glucose. Don’t worry about the pathway stuff here. All I want you to know is: PEP carboxykinase activity is down if we’re fed, and it’s up if we’re fasting and want to make glucose. • Pyruvate carboxylase is a gluconeogenic enzyme that converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate, so that oxaloacetate, via PEP carboxykinase, can go back to PEP, and ultimately up to glucose. Once again, don’t worry about the pathway stuff. Just know the pyruvate carboxylase is down in the fed state and up in the fasting state.

rapidFireQAs.q: 20M + eats turkey dinner. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for activity of glycogen synthase, phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK-2), glucose-6-phosphatase, and pyruvate dehydrogenase?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ Glycogen synthase, ↑ PFK-2, ↓ glucose-6-phosphatase, ↑ pyruvate dehydrogenase. — Glycogen synthase is up because we have glycogenesis in the fed state (so far not hard). • Normally in glycolysis, fructose-6-phosphate (F6P) is converted to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (F-1,6- BP) via PFK-1, the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis. However, some F6P can be shunted into a side pathway, via PFK-2, into F-2,6-BP. The latter is a positive allosteric regulator of PFK-1, thereby driving glycolysis forward. Once again, don’t freak out. What I want you to know is simply this: o Are we fed? Yes. Okay, F-2,6-BP production and PFK2 activity are up. o No, we’re fasting. Okay, F-2,6-BP production and PFK2 activity are down. • Glucose-6-phosphatase is a gluconeogenic enzyme that converts glucose-6-phosphate in the liver back into glucose (deficient in von Gierke disease). We would expect gluconeogenesis to be decreased in the fed state. • Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate (last molecule in glycolysis) into acetyl-CoA for entrance into the TCA cycle. Activity is increased in the fed state. Do not confuse this with pyruvate carboxylase, which is a gluconeogenic enzyme that converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate, so that oxaloacetate can be ultimately sent back to glucose.

rapidFireQAs.q: 10F + viral infection + polyuria + polydipsia. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for GLUT-4 expression, lipolysis, glucokinase activity, serine-threonine kinase activity, and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ GLUT-4 expression, ↑ lipolysis, ↓ glucokinase activity, ↓ serine-threonine kinase activity, ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis. — The patient has DKA. Insulin is deficient. • Insulin normally upregulates GLUT-4, which allows glucose to enter cells. If insulin is low, GLUT-4 expression is low. • Since insulin is low and cells are unable to uptake glucose as efficiently, energy must be produced in other ways. Lipolysis, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis are all increased. • Insulin upregulates glucokinase in the liver. Since insulin is low in DKA, glucokinase activity is also low. • USMLE wants you to know insulin increases activity of MAP tyrosine kinases and serine-threonine kinases. If insulin is deficient, activity is reduced for both of these. • When proteins are broken down within the cell, they can be tagged with ubiquitin in order to be sent to the proteasome. Insulin is anabolic and increases protein synthesis, not breakdown. If insulin is low, we’d get more protein breakdown in order to liberate free amino acids for energy. Therefore, low insulin means more ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis.

rapidFireQAs.q: A researcher is comparing glucokinase from a liver cell with hexokinase from a skeletal muscle cell. In terms of glucose processing, what is the Km and Vmax (i.e., ↑ or ↓) of glucokinase compared to hexokinase?
rapidFireQAs.a: Glucokinase has ↑ Km and ↑ Vmax compared to hexokinase. — ↑ Km = lower affinity; ↓ Km = higher affinity. • ↑ Vmax = higher capacity; ↓ Vmax = lower capacity. • In other words, glucokinase has both lower affinity and greater capacity for glucose than hexokinase. • Hexokinase is expressed by cells throughout the body. Glucokinase is predominantly just the liver. • The reason glucokinase has lower affinity for glucose is because we don’t want the liver taking up glucose when blood levels are low. We’d want cells throughout the body to preferentially get that glucose for energy utilization. If the liver takes it up, it will store it as glycogen. We don’t want that unless levels are high, so it’s good that glucokinase doesn’t bind glucose as easily as hexokinase. • But when glucose is high (meaning insulin goes up), we now want the liver to buffer out some of that glucose and convert it to glycogen for storage, so glucokinase gets activated by insulin. The liver converts glucose into glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), via glucokinase. G6P can then be converted to G1P in order to be polymerized into glycogen via glycogen synthase. • In addition, we need glucokinase to be able to process large amounts of glucose because it’s specifically activated when blood levels are high. So the capacity of glucokinase for glucose is greater than hexokinase.

Glucokinase is predominantly just the liver. • The reason glucokinase has lower affinity for glucose is because we don’t want the liver taking up glucose when blood levels are low. We’d want cells throughout the body to preferentially get that glucose for energy utilization. If the liver takes it up, it will store it as glycogen. We don’t want that unless levels are high, so it’s good that glucokinase doesn’t bind glucose as easily as hexokinase. • But when glucose is high (meaning insulin goes up), we now want the liver to buffer out some of that glucose and convert it to glycogen for storage, so glucokinase gets activated by insulin. The liver converts glucose into glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), via glucokinase. G6P can then be converted to G1P in order to be polymerized into glycogen via glycogen synthase. • In addition, we need glucokinase to be able to process large amounts of glucose because it’s specifically activated when blood levels are high. So the capacity of glucokinase for glucose is greater than hexokinase.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + lost in the woods for 3 weeks + only consumed water and occasional berries; BMI is 27; he is found by family who gives him a big meal. Following the consumption of food, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for expected acute changes in his serum K+ and serum PO43-?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ K+ , ↓ PO43- . — Refeeding syndrome can occur when a patient consumes food following days to weeks of starvation. • BMI can be low, normal, or high in refeeding syndrome. Do not be confused if BMI is not low. • Hypophosphatemia is the primary disturbance the USMLE wants you to know about. Rapid synthesis of glycolytic intermediates will trap phosphate and deplete serum levels. • Hypokalemia can also occur due to a spike in insulin, which will drive potassium into cells. • Patients must be monitored for electrolyte disturbances closely during refeeding in order to prevent arrhythmia.

rapidFireQAs.q: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a chronic cough that is worse at night and productive of thick white sputum. He is at the 3rd percentile for weight and height. Physical examination shows clubbing of the fingers. Chest auscultation shows diffuse inspiratory crackles and hyperresonance. The patient has a healthy 6-year-old sister. Which of the following represents the likelihood of this patient’s sister being a carrier of this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 2 of 3. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition on chromosome 7. There is a one-half chance each parent will pass his or her mutated allele to the offspring. In the following Punnett square, “A” refers to a non-diseased wild-type allele; “a” refers to a diseased allele. Since the sister is healthy (i.e., phenotypically normal), we know she can’t possibly be “aa,” so we can eliminate that. This leaves us with only three possibilities: AA + 2(Aa). 2(Aa) / 3 total possibilities = 2/3 chance of being a carrier. Bottom line: Phenotypically normal siblings of patients with AR disorders bear a 2/3 chance of being a carrier. This is an important genetics ratio you need to memorize for USMLE, as the exam will often ask harder questions, where knowing this ratio is a mere component of, rather than answer to, the question
options: F) There is no chance the patient’s sister is a carrier

rapidFireQAs.q: A 34-year-old woman presents to preconception counseling with her husband. Her family history is remarkable for a brother who died at the age of 3 from deficiency of a-L-iduronidase. Her husband’s family history is unremarkable. If the frequency of disease in the general population is approximately 1 in 100,000 for this condition, what is the probability this couple will have a son with the disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) 1/1900. First solve for carrier frequency in general population (husband’s carrier risk): Hardy-Weinberg equation: 1 = p2 + 2pq + q2 , where p + q = 1. q2 = 1/100,000 So q = √1/100,000 = 1/316. So p = 1 – (1/316) ≈ 1. 2pq = 2 x 1 x 1/316 = 1/158 = carrier frequency in general population. Next solve for chance the patient (mom) is a carrier: Hurler syndrome is an AR disorder. As per question #1, there is a 2/3 a phenotypically normal patient is a carrier of an AR disorder if he or she has a sibling with the disorder. Now solve for the risk this couple would have a child who has the AR disease: 2/3 (chance mom is carrier) x 1/158 (chance dad is carrier) x 1/4 (chance of aa) in Punnett square = 2/1896. However the question asked what is the chance the couple will have a son with the disease, so now we multiply by 1/2 (chance of having a son). This would be the same for daughters because this is an AR disorder. So 2/1896 x 1/2 = 1/1896 ≈ 1/1900. The USMLE will often give you conditions where q2 is, e.g., 1/10,000, so q is easier to solve for (1/100), without the need for decimals

rapidFireQAs.q: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mom for yellow discoloration of his eyes she first noticed this morning. He recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection. Serum studies show: Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL Hematocrit 30.9% Total bilirubin 4.0 mg/dL Direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL A peripheral blood smear is shown: The boy’s parents would like to have two more children. What is the probability that both children will carry the same diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 1 of 16. The diagnosis is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, an X-linked recessive disorder. Unless in the rare event of heavily skewed lyonization (X-inactivation), only boys will have the disorder. The patient has hemolysis precipitated by viral infection. The smear shows Heinz bodies (oxidized, precipitated hemoglobin) and bite cells (degmacytes; partially phagocytosed RBCs). The mother must be a carrier for the disorder (i.e., she has one X chromosome with the mutation). The chance of her having another son is 1/2. The chance of her passing the mutation-laden X- chromosome to this son is 1/2. So the chance of having another son with the disease is 1/4. The chance therefore of two sons in a row with the disease would be 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16 = the chance this couple’s next two children will have G6PD deficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: A newborn male dies shortly after birth due to multiple organ system abnormalities. Autopsy shows an apparent transformation of lumbar vertebrae to a thoracic identity. Which of the following mechanisms relating to HOX gene may best explain this observation at the thoracic level?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) Expression of a HOX gene normally transcribed only cranially. HOX genes are involved in the patterning of an embryo along the head-tail axis – i.e., they encode the characteristic positions of body parts, ensuring development at correct locations. For example, lumbar vertebrae develop specifically at the lumbar level, and not at the sacral, thoracic, or cervical levels, because HOX genes ensure this specific type of developmental patterning. If lumbar vertebrae are transformed into a thoracic identity – i.e., if vertebrae at the lumbar location have developed to appear like thoracic ones – then one possible mechanism is that thoracic HOX genes were inadvertently expressed at the lumbar location. Since thoracic HOX genes are cranial to the lumbar ones, the transformation of lumbar vertebrae into thoracic ones means that genes normally expressed only superior (cranial) got expressed at an inferior (caudal) location. Choice B would refer to the transformation of thoracic vertebrae into lumbar ones
options: A) Alteration in transcription factor binding sites at the thoracic-lumbar vertebral junction
B) Expression of a HOX gene normally transcribed only caudally
C) Expression of a HOX gene normally transcribed only cranially
D) Insufficient expression of a HOX gene at the lumbar level
E) Insufficient expression of a HOX enhancer sequence at the thoracic level

rapidFireQAs.q: A 42-year-old woman presents to the physician with a 3-month history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She has a history of recurrent epistaxis since childhood. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 75%. A photograph of the patient’s tongue is shown. The patient’s husband does not have a family history of the condition. What is the probability the patient and her husband will have a daughter who is a carrier?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) 0. The diagnosis is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu), an autosomal dominant disorder. The image shown is a telangiectasia of the tongue. The USMLE is also known to show an image of nailbed telangiectasias. This patient has high-output cardiac failure secondary to a pulmonary arteriovenous fistula, which can present in adulthood. Telangiectasias of the nasal mucosa resulting in recurrent epistaxis since childhood are characteristic. Telangiectasias within the GI tract can cause GI bleeding and anemia. Autosomal dominant disorders do not have a carrier state, since only one mutation results in disease phenotype. Carrier states are only possible in AR and XR disorders. Even if a disease has incomplete penetrance (i.e., not all patients with diseased genotype bear the diseased phenotype), a patient with a dominant mutation would still not be considered a carrier. He or she would be said to have an AD disorder, albeit with reduced penetrance. The husband cannot be a carrier, since HHT is an AD disorder and he does not have family history

rapidFireQAs.q: A 39-year-old man and his wife have two sons with history of retinoblastoma and a daughter with osteosarcoma. Neither the patient nor his wife have history of health problems. The patient is identified as II-5 on the pedigree. Which of the following best explains the reason for the patient’s health?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) Incomplete penetrance. This patient’s (II-5) family has congenital retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma in infancy and/or osteosarcoma later in life are most characteristic of the condition. Congenital retinoblastoma is an autosomal dominant disorder with incomplete penetrance. Incomplete penetrance is when not everyone with the diseased genotype bears the diseased phenotype (i.e., not everyone with the disease expresses it); this is sometimes referred to as “skipping a generation,” and also applies to the BRCA genes. Variable expressivity, in contrast, implies 100% penetrance – i.e., everyone with the disease expresses it in some form. The difference is the mere severity in which family members manifest the condition. NF1 is a classic example, where everyone with the disease has it, but whilst one family member might only present with axillary and groin freckling, another might develop pheochromocytoma and optic glioma. If the NBME/USMLE gives you a pedigree that looks like incomplete penetrance (as with this question), but the diagnosis in the family is NF1, choose variable expressivity, not incomplete penetrance. A patient with minimal disease severity in NF1 might not report having it. Heteroplasmy is a phenomenon seen in mitochondrial disorders, an inheritance pattern characterized by strict maternal transmission (i.e., mothers transmit disease to sons and daughters; fathers never transmit disease), where varying amounts of diseased mitochondria are passed to the next generation, resulting in offspring with disease of varying severity. This is due to the mother’s oocytes carrying thousands of copies of mitochondrial DNA, where the oocytes differ in the ratios of diseased mitochondria they contain. Do not confuse this with variable expressivity, which instead refers to non-mitochondrial disorders, where a chromosomal mutation can result in varying severity of disease. Somatic mosaicism is when only a percentage of an individual’s “body cells” (somatic = body) contain a diseased genotype. This results from a post-fertilization mitotic error, where the mutation results in only some of the organism’s cells being affected by disease. Classic examples for USMLE would be mosaic Turner or Down, where the answer is “post-fertilization mitotic error.” Sturge- Weber is also an example of somatic mosaicism. Germline (gonadal) mosaicism is when the spermatogonia or oogonia of one of the parents carry a mutation, but the somatic (body) cells do not. The result is that offspring can have an AD disorder despite the parents not being affected. Germline mosaicism is the answer classically for achondroplasia – i.e., the parents are normal but the child has the disease. The child will have 100% of his or her body cells affected because the original mutation was in the spermatogonia or oogonia of the parent, rather than occurring post-mitotically, as with somatic mosaicism. If the USMLE does not give achondroplasia, they will say two phenotypically normal parents have two children with an AD disorder, implying there is a germline mutation in one of the parents (usually the father)

rapidFireQAs.q: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents for a follow-up appointment. He has a history since birth of recurrent Staph, Candida, and viral infections. Examination shows scanty lymph nodes and tonsils and absent thymic shadow. Molecular analysis shows deficiency of adenosine deaminase. The boy’s parents are planning to have more children. What is the probability that they will have a daughter with this molecular defect?
rapidFireQAs.a: G) 1 in 8, since this condition is autosomal recessive H) 2 in 3, since this condition is autosomal dominant I) 2 in 3, since this condition is autosomal recessive. The diagnosis is severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). There are two main types of SCID: - XR: common gamma chain mutation, or IL-2 receptor deficiency - AR: adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency Since the patient has ADA deficiency, we know he has the AR, not XR, type of SCID. This means there is a 1/4 chance the couple will have another child with AR SCID, and a 1/8 chance they will have a daughter with AR SCID (i.e., 1/4 chance of next child with SCID x 1/2 chance of having a daughter). The ratio 2/3 refers to the probability that a phenotypically normal sibling of a patient with an AR disorder is a carrier for the disease. If the patient in the vignette had common gamma chain mutation or IL-2 receptor deficiency (both XR SCID), then the answer would be zero percent

rapidFireQAs.q: A child (III-1 in the pedigree) has a history of a condition characterized by self-mutilation, aggressive behavior, and orange-red, sandy crystals in the diaper. Assuming the mating partner of II-5 is genotypically normal, what is the probability that individual III-4 develops a similar condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Zero percent. The diagnosis is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder, caused by deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This enzyme is required for the recycling of purines. Deficiency leads to gout due to overproduction of uric acid. Vignettes will give young boys who exhibit self-mutilation and red-orange sand-like crystals in their diapers. XR diseases cannot be transmitted from father to son, so even if II-5 in the pedigree had the condition, he wouldn’t be able to transfer it anyway. If we consider daughter III-3, there is also a zero percent chance she would be a carrier for the condition as well, since II-5 does not have the disease
options: F) Cannot be determined without carrier status of mating partner of II-5

rapidFireQAs.q: A 54-year-old woman (II-1) presents to the cardiologist for a follow-up examination. She has an ejection fraction of 35% and a dilated cardiac silhouette. She has chronic joint pain of her hands and an occasional sore knee managed with indomethacin. Fasting blood glucose is 130 mg/dL. If the disease frequency of this condition is 1/400 in the general population, what is the probability that III-1 has the disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 19/1200. The diagnosis is hereditary hemochromatosis, an autosomal recessive condition, caused by mutations in the HFE gene on chromosome 6. This results in iron overload caused by an inability to shut off iron absorption in the duodenum. Since individual II-1 has the disease, we know that I-1 is a carrier. In addition, we also know that phenotypically normal siblings of individuals with AR disorders have a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, since “aa” is eliminated from the Punnett square (because they don’t have the disease). This means there is a 2/3 chance II-5 is a carrier. Now we need to calculate the probability that the mating partner of II-5 is a carrier. Using our annoying as Hardy-Weinberg equation: 1 = p2 + 2pq + q2, where q2 = 1/400, and q = 1/20. Since 1 = p + q, p = 19/20. 2pq (carrier frequency) therefore = 2(19/20)(1/20) = 38/400 = 19/200 in general population. Now we calculate the chance that III-1 has the disease: 2/3 (chance II-5 father is carrier) x 19/200 (chance mother is carrier from general population) x 1/4 chance of “aa” within the Punnett square = 38/2400 = 19/1200. “Bronze” diabetes is a classic presentation for this condition, characterized by hyperpigmentation of the skin (due to hemosiderin deposition), diabetes mellitus (due to iron deposition in the tail of the pancreas), and various other findings, such as pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease), cardiomyopathy (dilated or restrictive), and infertility (due to hypothalamic or testicular iron deposition). This presentation is slightly harder because hyperpigmentation is omitted from the stem, but the patient has dilated cardiomyopathy, pseudogout, and diabetes mellitus. The two biggest risk factors for pseudogout are hereditary hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism. Pseudogout usually presents as either a monoarthritis of a large joint, such as the knee, or as a polyarthritis resembling osteoarthritis (OA). If the vignette gives you, e.g., Bouchard or Heberden nodes in a patient with hemochromatosis or primary hyperparathyroidism, the diagnosis is pseudogout, not OA. Some students will ask, “But if we are forced to choose which cardiomyopathy it is, dilated or restrictive, which one is it?” The answer is: whichever one they give you, since the presentations are disparate. DCM presents with S3, enlarged silhouette, and decreased ejection fraction. RCM presents with S4, JVD, a normal silhouette, and normal ejection fraction

rapidFireQAs.q: A 36-year-old woman with HIV is undergoes HLA screening prior to commencement of abacavir as part of her anti-retroviral therapy. Genetic analysis confirms the homozygous presence of HLA B*5701 alleles. What is the likelihood this patient’s brother is also homozygous for the same alleles?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) 25%. HLA genes are inherited as haplotypes, which are a set of alleles inherited from each parent. Each parent will have two haplotypes. The HLA B*5701 allele would be carried within one of the haplotypes of each parent. The patient is homozygous for the HLA B*5701 allele. This means she has the haplotype 1 / haplotype 3 combination. Since there are only four combinations, there is a 1/4 (25%) chance her brother would also have homozygous HLA B*5701 alleles. Abacavir is known to a cause a hypersensitivity-like reaction in patients with HLA B*5701 positivity. Screening for this HLA haplotype is required prior to commencement of abacavir

rapidFireQAs.q: A 21-year-old woman presents to the physician for a two-month history of weakness, headache, and blurry vision. Serum studies show a hemoglobin of 18.5 g/dL. Serum calcium is 10.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 1+ RBCs. CT of the abdomen confirms the diagnosis. In addition, cysts are seen within the pancreas. Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance of this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Autosomal dominant. The diagnosis is von Hippel-Lindau (VHL), an autosomal dominant disorder on chromosome 3, which results in failure of degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). VHL is characterized by renal cell carcinoma (can become bilateral), pancreatic cysts, and cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas. Renal cell carcinoma can present with polycythemia (due to EPO secretion) and hypercalcemia (paraneoplastic PTHrp secretion; similar to squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, yes). Blurry vision and headache can be a result of hyperviscosity syndrome due to the high hemoglobin. The former could also be seen in retinal hemangioblastoma. VHL is one of the phakomatoses (neurocutaneous disorders). The other high-yield ones for USMLE are neurofibromatosis 1 and 2 (NF1, NF2), tuberous sclerosis (TSC), and Sturge-Weber. NF1, NF2, TSC, and VHL are all autosomal dominant. Sturge-Weber is not inherited and is a somatic mosaicism disorder (post-fertilization mitotic error). NF1 (chromosome 17) is characterized by neurofibromas, axillary and groin freckling, café au lait spots (hyperpigmented macules), pheochromocytoma, optic glioma, and “weird” CNS tumors such as oligodendroglioma and ependymoma. NF2 (chromosome 22) presents as acoustic schwannoma (can be bilateral) and meningioma. TSC (chromosomes 9 and 16; coding for hamartin and tuberin proteins, respectively) presents as periventricular nodules (tubers), adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas; reddish-peach-colored papules in the nasolabial folds and on the bridge of the nose), cardiac rhabdomyoma, subungual fibromas, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, renal angiomyolipoma, ashleaf spots (hypopigmented macules), and shagreen patches (hyperpigmented velvety lesions). Vignettes will often be children presenting with seizures (i.e., writing movements during sleep) due to the tubers. Sturge-Weber presents with Port wine stain birthmark (nevus flammeus; but can also present as violaceous papules in a temporal distribution), glaucoma, leptomeningeal angiomas, and seizures

rapidFireQAs.q: A 22-year-old woman presents to the physician for a two-month history of fatigue, mild cognitive degeneration, and clumsiness. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and a resting tremor of her left hand. Serum studies show elevated hepatic transaminases. Hemoglobin is 9.5 g/dL. Blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance of this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: B) Autosomal recessive. The diagnosis is Wilson disease, an autosomal recessive condition on chromosome 13, characterized by an inability to excrete copper into bile and resultant copper overload. Patients have increased urinary copper and decreased serum ceruloplasmin (copper-binding protein). The latter results in increased free serum copper that accumulates within RBCs, leading to hemolysis and spherocytosis. Spherocytes are not limited to hereditary spherocytosis (which is autosomal dominant). The USMLE wants you to know they are frequently seen in the setting of drug- and infection-induced hemolysis. They are also seen in hemolytic anemia in Wilson disease. (Should be noted tangentially that they are not seen in G6PD deficiency; bite cells are seen instead) Wilson disease can present as Parkinsonism in a young patient (i.e., unilateral resting tremor, bradykinesia, shuffling gait, etc.), and hence is known as a Parkinson-plus disorder (i.e., appears like Parkinson disease but is not). This is due to copper deposition within the basal ganglia. Other HY Parkinson-plus syndromes for USMLE are progressive supranuclear palsy, normal pressure hydrocephalus, Lewy body dementia, MPTP-induced Parkinsonism, and antipsychotic-induced Parkinsonism. Liver disease and cirrhosis are also important findings in Wilson. LFTs may be variable depending on stage of liver failure. Cirrhotic patients will have elevated prothrombin time (PT). Kayser-Fleischer rings are often too easy and omitted from USMLE vignettes. These are copper rings seen with Descemet membrane of the cornea. The USMLE might give you a vignette of Wilson disease, and then the answer is, “Perform a slit-lamp examination.” Treatment of Wilson disease is with penicillamine, a copper chelator. Trientine and zinc supplements may also be used. Bottom line: The heavy metal disorders – Wilson and hemochromatosis – are autosomal recessive

rapidFireQAs.q: A 15-year-old boy has a 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion, muscle weakness, and worsening exercise tolerance. Vitals are within normal limits. Physical examination shows bilateral ptosis. Muscle strength is 3/5 in all extremities. A pedigree is shown. The patient is represented by III-10. Which of the following best explains the combination of findings in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) Heteroplasmy. This patient has a mitochondrial disorder. This is evidenced by the classic constellation of lactic acidosis, hypotonia, and ear and/or eye problem. Mitochondrial inheritance is strictly maternal – i.e., only females can pass disease to offspring; males cannot transmit disease. This is because the mitochondrial genes are separate from the chromosomal ones. The oocytes of the female contain thousands of copies mitochondrial genes, which are the source of mitochondrial DNA in the resultant zygote. The sperm does not contribute mitochondrial DNA to the zygote. Each oocyte contains a different proportion/fraction of diseased mitochondria. Depending on the fraction of diseased versus normal mitochondrial DNA, the resultant offspring will bear varying disease severity. This is referred to as heteroplasmy. Allelic heterogeneity refers to different alleles resulting in the same disease. Cystic fibrosis is a classic example, where a large number of possible mutations within the CFTR gene are known to cause disease, with DF508 being most common. The Sweat chloride test is more accurate than genotyping for CF because common CFTR screening panels will only detect upwards of 96% of likely mutations. Sweat chloride test, however, will be positive in all patients with CF. Anticipation refers to the propensity for trinucleotide repeat (TNR) disorders presenting earlier and more severe with each successive generation. This is due to an expansion of the number of repeats with each generation. For example, Huntington disease may present in a male at age 36 who has 55 repeats, whereas in his mother it presented at age 44, and she only had 48 repeats (40 or more CAG cause disease). Chimerism is a phenomenon seen in some animal species, i.e., mice and cats, where more than two parents contribute DNA to the offspring. This is due to fusion of embryos. Chimerism is not seen in humans. Complete penetrance is when 100% of those with a diseased genotype go on to develop the diseased phenotype. Incomplete penetrance is “skipping a generation,” where some individuals with a diseased genotype do not develop the diseased phenotype. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, congenital retinoblastoma, and BRCA mutations are classic examples of incomplete penetrance. Pleiotropy is when one gene results in many phenotypic effects – e.g., TP53 mutations resulting in Li- Fraumeni syndrome can result in many different types of cancers (e.g., pancreatic, colon). Another example is phenylketonuria (PKU), where a mutation in phenylalanine hydroxylase can result in partial albinism, mental retardation, and musty body odor

rapidFireQAs.q: A 24-year-old woman presents to the physician with an ongoing history of heavy menses and epistaxis. Serum studies show: Platelet count: 200,000/µL Platelet aggregation studies: Normal Prothrombin time: 12 seconds Partial thromboplastin time: 38 seconds Bleeding time: 9 minutes Ristocetin assay: Suppressed Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
rapidFireQAs.a: F) Von Willebrand disease. Student says, “Wait, how is this a genetics question. I’m confused.” The USMLE will sometimes weave genetics knowledge into questions rather than asking you for inheritance patterns directly. This type of question is one of the highest yield applications of inheritance patterns. Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is autosomal dominant. Hemophilia A and B are both X-linked recessive. Since this vignette is a female patient, even if you aren’t sure of the hematologic diagnosis, if you know the inheritance patterns, you can instantly eliminate the hemophilias because the patient is not male. Von Willebrand disease will almost always present as a combination of one clotting factor problem (i.e., menorrhagia, excessive bleeding with tooth extraction) and one platelet problem (petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis). If the vignette unexpectedly gives you, e.g., only menorrhagia, you will be able to diagnose definitively based on the laboratory findings. Von Willebrand factor (vWF) helps enable platelet adhesion by bridging glycoprotein Ib on platelets to vascular endothelium. The ristocetin assay will be abnormal in patients with impaired platelet adhesion. This means vWD and Bernard-Soulier disease (deficiency of GpIb) both have abnormal ristocetin assays. Von Willebrand factor plays no role in platelet aggregation, where Gp IIb/IIIa on adjacent platelets are bridged together by fibrinogen. This means platelet aggregation studies are normal in vWD. Bleeding time (normally 2-7 minutes) is increased if there is a platelet problem. Since platelet adhesion is disrupted in vWD, bleeding time is always increased. Von Willebrand factor has an auxiliary role in helping to stabilize factor VIII in plasma. This means about half the time partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) will be increased. Normal range is 25-40 seconds. Since this stabilization of factor VIII is not the primary role of vWF, aPTT is normal in about half of USMLE questions. Students normally this up, as they erroneously think aPTT is always increased in addition to BT. But aPTT is increased in only about half of questions. Prothrombin time (PT) is normal in vWD because factor VIII is in the intrinsic, not the extrinsic, pathway. Platelet count is normal in vWD because there is no mechanism for platelet destruction. There is merely impaired binding of Gp Ib on platelets to vascular endothelium. Hemophilia A and B are deficiency of factors VIII and IX, respectively. The textbook vignette will be a school-age male with hemarthrosis. aPTT will be elevated. BT and PT are normal. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is deficiency of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa on platelets, resulting in impaired aggregation. The ristocetin assay is normal in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP; aka immune thrombocytopenia purpura) is an isolated thrombocytopenia caused by antibodies against Gp IIb/IIIa on platelets. The classic presentation is a school-age kid or a woman 30s-40s with epistaxis or random bruising. Only BT is increased, and platelet count is always down. Vitamin K deficiency presents with normal bleeding time, and increased PT and aPTT. Vitamin K does not affect platelets. It is a cofactor the for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase. Deficiency leads to impaired clotting due to inability to activate factors II, VII, IX, and X (as well as anti-clotting proteins C and S)

rapidFireQAs.q: A 7-year-old girl with happy personality and mental retardation undergoes karyotypic analysis that does not reveal a deletion of the expected UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. Which of the following findings via fluorescent in situ hybridization is most likely to confirm the diagnosis in this child?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) Paternal uniparental disomy. The diagnosis is Angelman syndrome (AS; aka “happy puppet” syndrome), caused usually by maternal mutation or deletion of the paternally imprinted UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. It can also be caused by paternal uniparental disomy. Imprinting is a normal genomic-wide process via which certain genes demonstrate a silencing of one allele from one parent. Maternal imprinting = allele coming from mom is silenced; therefore, only dad’s allele is expressed. Paternal imprinting = allele coming from dad is silenced; therefore, only mom’s allele is expressed. The UBE3A gene associated with Angelman syndrome is normally paternally imprinted, meaning even though two UBE3A alleles are inherited (one from each parent), only mom’s is normally expressed. If there is a maternal deletion or mutation, then even if the allele received from dad is normal, because dad’s allele is silenced, disease phenotype occurs because the child can only express the mutated/deleted maternal one. “Mom is not an Angel” is the mnemonic for Angelman syndrome. Mom is not an angel because her gene is deleted (and the one received from dad is silenced). This patient, however, was found to not have a deletion on karyotypic analysis. This means that maternal deletion/mutation was not the mechanism for disease here. Uniparental disomy is when both alleles are erroneously inherited from one parent. Angelman syndrome can also be caused by paternal uniparental disomy, where both alleles are inherited from dad (but are silenced). If both alleles are inherited from dad, even if they are both normal/not mutated, because both coming from dad would be silenced, this leaves no maternal allele that can be expressed, therefore resulting in disease. AS = paternal imprinting + maternal gene deletion, OR paternal uniparental disomy. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is another condition that demonstrates similar disease mechanisms as Angelman syndrome. PWS is characterized by hyperphagia (resulting in obesity) and mental retardation. PWS does not involve UBE3A, but can be caused by many genes on chromosome 15. “Willi hates his dad” because dad’s gene is deleted/mutated (and mom’s is imprinted/silenced). PWS can also be caused by maternal uniparental disomy, where both alleles are inherited from mom (but are silenced). PWS = maternal imprinting + paternal gene deletion, OR maternal uniparental disomy

rapidFireQAs.q: A 4-year-old boy with a congenital enzyme deficiency is brought to the pediatrician for a follow-up examination. The disease frequency is approximately 1 in 200,000 in males. A bone marrow aspirate is shown. Which of the following is the expected prevalence of heterozygous females for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) 1 in 100,000. Congenital sideroblastic anemia is an X-linked recessive disorder. The image shows a ringed sideroblast on Prussian blue staining. For XR disorders, disease frequency in males = q. In females, disease frequency = q2 . If the frequency in males is 1/200,000 = q, then disease frequency in females = (1/200,000)2 . This question is not asking for the disease frequency in females, however. It is asking for carrier (heterozygote) frequency. Using Hardy-Weinberg: 1 = p2 + 2pq + q2 = (p + q), since q = 1/200,000, p = 199,999/200,000 ≈ 1. 2pq = 2 x 1 x 1/200,000 = 1/100,000 = carrier frequency in females. This only applies to females because males cannot be carriers for XR disorders. So carrier frequency in females = carrier frequency in the general population for XR disorders. In summary, for XR disorders: - Disease frequency in males = q - Disease frequency in females = q2 - Carrier (heterozygote) frequency in females = 2pq

rapidFireQAs.q: A 6-year-old girl has had recurrent pneumonias since birth. Her mother reports that her stools appear to float and are foul-smelling. She is at the 5th percentile for height and weight. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles. Chest x-ray shows increased bronchovascular markings. She is III-3 in the pedigree below. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the pattern of inheritance in this family?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) Autosomal recessive with high heterozygote frequency. The diagnosis is cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, which result in a misfolded CFTR chloride channel. In order for cousins III-2 and III-3 to have the disease despite the absence of disease in other family members, the implication is that the carrier (heterozygosity) rate is high. The misfolded CFTR chloride channel remains sequestered within the rough endoplasmic reticulum (i.e., it is not transported to the cell surface). CFTR channel is cAMP-mediated and ATP-gated. Bottom line: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. Know this inheritance pattern for USMLE

B) Autosomal dominant with variable expressivity

rapidFireQAs.q: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents for progressive muscle weakness. Physical examination shows scoliosis and enlargement of the calf muscles. When positioned on his stomach and asked to stand up, the boy appears to “walk” to a standing position using his arms. If the boy’s parents have more children, what is the probability they will have a child who is a carrier for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) 1 in 4. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder usually caused by frameshift mutations in the DMD gene coding for dystrophin. Dystrophin is a protein required for maintaining the integrity of the muscle cell by linking its cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Boys cannot be carriers for this condition because it is XR; only girls can be carriers. The chance that the parents have another child who is a girl is 1/2. There is then a 1/2 chance that the mother, who is a carrier, passes the X-chromosome with the DMD mutation to the daughter. Therefore, 1/2 (chance of daughter) x 1/2 (chance of passing mutated X) = 1 in 4 chance of having a child who is a carrier for this condition. Physical examination in Duchenne frequently shows pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles. The enlargement of the calves is not pure muscle; fibroadipose deposition ensues leading to weakness. Most boys lose the ability to walk by adolescence. Gower’s maneuver is the use of the arms to stand up from a prone position. This is in order to compensate for weakness of the pelvic muscles. Becker muscular dystrophy is a less severe form of Duchenne that is also an XR disorder of the DMD gene. Unlike Duchenne, which is classically caused by frameshift mutations and presents within the first few years of life, Becker is frequently caused by missense mutations and presents in late adolescence or early adulthood

There is then a 1/2 chance that the mother, who is a carrier, passes the X-chromosome with the DMD mutation to the daughter. Therefore, 1/2 (chance of daughter) x 1/2 (chance of passing mutated X) = 1 in 4 chance of having a child who is a carrier for this condition. Becker muscular dystrophy is a less severe form of Duchenne that is also an XR disorder of the DMD gene. Unlike Duchenne, which is classically caused by frameshift mutations and presents within the first few years of life, Becker is frequently caused by missense mutations and presents in late adolescence or early adulthood.

rapidFireQAs.q: A phenotypically normal 24-year-old woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder that is lethal in utero (i.e., results in spontaneous abortion). Which of the following is the probability that the next child she gives birth to is a carrier for this disorder?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) 1 in 3. Half of the males this patient conceives will be spontaneously aborted in utero, as there is a 1/2 chance a male child will receive the lethal X-chromosome. In contrast, no females will be aborted in utero because this is an XR condition. Our possible combinations for conception are: - Normal female (non-carrier): XX - Carrier female: XX - Normal male: XY - Diseased male (lethal): XY This means there is a 2:1 ratio of females:males who will be birthed by this patient, where 1:3 of the children overall will be carriers

rapidFireQAs.q: A 28-year-old male presents to the physician for a 3-day history of dark urine. Dipstick shows 2+ blood. He has had many such occurrences in the past. The patient wears hearing aids and glasses. Renal biopsy shows an apparent splitting of the glomerular basement membrane. Which of the following inheritance patterns best describes this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) X-linked. The diagnosis is Alport syndrome, an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the gene for collagen type IV. The vignette will give you a male with hematuria who has an ear and/or eye problem. Renal biopsy will show splitting of the basement membrane with a characteristic “basket-weave” appearance. Patients can develop sensorineural hearing loss and diminished visual acuity due to abnormal collagen IV in the inner ear and lens of the eye, respectively. Hematuria results from loss of glomerular basement membrane integrity. Do not confuse Alport with Goodpasture syndrome, which is instead caused by antibodies against type IV collagen. Goodpasture will present as a male 20s-40s with hematuria and hemoptysis. Renal biopsy shows linear immunofluorescence due to anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM; type IV collagen) antibodies

rapidFireQAs.q: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his mother for a follow-up examination. Physical examination shows everted ears and a long jaw. Testicular volume is increased. Karyotypic analysis shows an expansion of 650 CGG repeats within the 5’ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this CGG expansion?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Decreased transcription. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by a CGG trinucleotide expansion within the FMR1 gene. Greater than 200 CGG repeats results in disease. Prominent, everted ears, a long, narrow jaw, and reduced IQ are characteristic of the phenotype. Males will also often have macroorchidism. The CGG repeat expansion results in hypermethylation of the FMR1 gene and resultant decreased binding of transcription factors and RNA polymerase II. The answer on the USMLE is “decreased transcription. rapidFireQAs.q: A family has many individuals with phenotypes characterized by hyperpigmented macules, axillary and groin freckling, iris hamartomas, pheochromocytoma, and optic glioma. Genetic analysis of chromosome 17 is performed. Patients III-3 and IV-4 in the pedigree bear disease phenotype but have an observed wild-type locus on the examined allele. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) Recombination. The diagnosis is neurofibromatosis type I (NF1), an autosomal dominant disorder on chromosome 17 demonstrating complete penetrance and variable expressivity. The wild-type (non-diseased) allele in this family is identified as A-B-C. The individuals with NF1 have the diseased D-E-F allele. However, patients III-3 and IV-4 are observed to have allele A-E-F, rather than D-E-F. This is because locus A from the wild-type allele replaced locus D on the diseased allele during meiosis-I, where chromatids exchange some genetic material and then separate. This is called recombination. The chance that two loci will undergo a recombination event is called the recombination fraction. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are when one base substitutes for another. These account for most variation among individuals. While an SNP could explain a random alteration in the diseased locus, it would not specifically account for the wild-type locus having become the one present on the diseased allele. Insertions, inversions, and transpositions are known chromosomal rearrangements, but the replacement of a diseased locus with a wild-type one is due to recombination during meiosis-I. An insertion might be observed as D-A-E-F instead of the D-E-F locus. A transposition is when a piece of genetic material from one part of the genome migrates and inserts itself elsewhere within the genome. If a transposition of a wild-type locus occurred, it would be observed as an insertion event. An inversion might be observed as D-F-E instead of D-E-F

rapidFireQAs.q: A 34-year-old woman presents to the physician for a lump she self-palpated in her right breast. Her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 40; her maternal aunt was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at the age of 37. Genetic testing is most likely to show a mutation in which of the following molecular processes?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) Recombinational double-stranded DNA repair. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes on chromosomes 17 and 13, respectively. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance (i.e., cancer phenotype can “skip” a generation). Mutations result in increased risk of breast cancer in both females and males, as well as gynecologic cancers in females and testicular cancer in males. Mutations in BRCA genes result in defective recombinational double-stranded DNA repair. This process normally involves the repair of DNA using complementary strands from homologous dsDNA. Base excision repair involves the removal of a single mutated base. This is the answer on the USMLE if the stem mentions glycosylases (i.e., glycosylase enzymes are required for this process). Nucleotide excision repair involves the removal of bulky DNA distortions, namely pyrimidine- pyrimidine dimers due to UV exposure. This is the answer on the USMLE for xeroderma pigmentosa. Mismatch repair involves the removal of an incorrect base inserted during DNA synthesis. The template strand is methylated; the newly synthesized strand is unmethylated. Mismatch repair enzymes identify the newly synthesized strand due to its lack of methylation and remove/replace the incorrect base. Mismatch repair is the answer on USMLE for Lynch syndrome (HNPCC). This presents as colonic polyps +/- gynecologic cancers or other organ system cancers, e.g., pancreatic or duodenal cancer. Defects in mismatch repair are sometimes referred to as “microsatellite instability.” The important genes are MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2. Slipped-strand mispairing is the answer on USMLE if there is an insertion or deletion of bases within strands of tandem repeats. For example, if there is a sequence of CCCCCCTA that erroneously becomes CCCCCCCTA, where a C was inserted, the type of repair that is needed here is slipped- strand mispairing

rapidFireQAs.q: An investigator is looking at a mutation sequence within the collagen type I gene of a patient with osteogenesis imperfecta. This sequence is compared to that of a healthy individual: Healthy individual: 5’-GAGCCCTA-3’ Osteogenesis imperfecta: 5’-GAGGCCTA-3’ This mutation allows for the creation of a diagnostic test using a restriction enzyme. Which of the following sequences most likely represents the cleavage site for the restriction enzyme?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 5’-GGCC-3’. Student says, “?” The USMLE wants you to know that restriction enzymes usually cleave along palindromic sequences. A palindrome is a sequence is one that is the same forward and backwards. 5’-GGCC-3’ becomes palindromic when paired with 3’-CCGG-5’ as dsDNA. The restriction enzyme will recognize this sequence and then cleave: Bottom line: if you get an obscure restriction enzyme question and are asked to identify a cleavage site, remember that palindromic sequences are preferred by these enzymes

rapidFireQAs.q: The frequency of an autosomal recessive disease in the population is 1/40,000. Frameshift mutations account for 30% of mutations at this locus; 70% are due to point mutations. The frequency of frameshift mutation carriers in the population is closest to which of the following?
rapidFireQAs.a: C) 3/1000. Using Hardy-Weinberg: 1= p2 + 2pq + q2 = p + q, q2 = 1/40,000. Therefore q = 1/200. Since p + q = 1, p = 199/200 ≈ 1. 2pq = 2 x 1 x 1/200 = 1/100 = carrier frequency in population. However, of the 1/100 in the population who are carriers, only 30% are frameshift mutation carriers. Therefore: 1/100 x 3/10 = 3/1000. If the question asked for point mutation carriers, we’d have: 1/100 x 7/10 = 7/1000. If that sounds confusing, think of it this way: since the carrier frequency in the population is 1/100, that’s the same as 10/1000. So 30% of 10/1000 = 3/1000 for frameshift mutation carriers, and 70% of 10/1000 = 7/1000 for point mutation carriers

rapidFireQAs.q: A 24-year-old woman needs to undergo a renal transplant secondary to long-standing history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis. She has a brother and sister. What is the probability that both her brother and sister will have human leukocyte antigen types that make them suitable donors?
rapidFireQAs.a: F) 1 in 16. As discussed earlier, HLA genes are inherited as haplotypes from each parent. There is a 1/4 chance that an individual’s full sibling will have the same HLAs (i.e., 1/2 chance of inheriting the same haplotype from mom x 1/2 chance of inheriting the same haplotype from dad). This question asks for the probability that both siblings are suitable donors. Therefore 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16

rapidFireQAs.q: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the GP by her mom because she has not yet had a menstrual period. Physical examination shows a vagina that is 3-cm long and ends in a blind pouch. Her breasts are Tanner stage 4 and there is coarse pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely karyotype of this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: B) 46XX. The diagnosis is Müllerian agenesis, which results in atresia of the vagina, cervix, uterus, and Fallopian tubes, as these structures are derived from the Müllerian ducts. The ovaries are not derived from the Müllerian ducts and thus are not affected. Normal secretion of hormones results in phenotypic female with normal Tanner stages. If the USMLE gives you this same exact presentation but tells you there is scanty or absent pubic and axillary hair, the answer is androgen insensitivity syndrome, not Müllerian agenesis. This is due to a defect in the androgen receptor, and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is needed for the development of external male sex characteristics. The patient will be a karyotypic male (46XY) but appear phenotypically female. In other words: Female teenager + normal Tanner stages + vagina ends in blind pouch + normal/coarse pubic/axillary hair: answer = Müllerian agenesis. Karyotype = 46XX (karyotypic female). Female teenager + normal Tanner stages + vagina ends in blind pouch + scanty/absent pubic/axillary hair: answer = androgen insensitivity syndrome. Karyotype = 46XY (karyotypic male). Turner syndrome (45X) usually presents as a short female (<5’1”) with a shield chest that is Tanner stage 1 or 2, cystic hygroma (webbed neck due to lymphatic insufficiency), and scattered nevi. Coarctation of the aorta and/or bicuspid aortic valve (aortic stenosis) may be seen. Patients with Turner present with streak ovaries and will not menstruate; this is colloquially referred to as “menopause before menarche.” USMLE wants you to know pregnancy is possible via IVF with donor oocytes (i.e., for behavioral questions, it is incorrect to outright say she cannot have a pregnancy). Klinefelter syndrome (47XXY) most often presents as a tall male with eunuchoid body shape (i.e., wide hips like a female) and small phallus and testes. Males cannot reproduce due to agenesis of the seminiferous tubules. 5a-reductase deficiency (46XY) is another common vignette. The enzyme normally converts testosterone → DHT. It frequently presents as “phallus at age 12,” where a 12- or 13-year-old girl grows four inches in the past four months and whose clitoris has elongated to 3-4 cm in length. This is due to a surge of testosterone during puberty that may overcome some of the enzyme deficiency, resulting in sufficient DHT for nascent external male sex characteristics. Another presentation will be a neonate born with ambiguous genitalia who is confirmed 46XY and who has male, but not female, genital ducts

rapidFireQAs.q: A 32-year-old woman presents to the physician for a one-week history of sore hands and knees. Physical examination shows an ulcer on the buccal mucosa. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL Hematocrit 31.5% WBC 4,500/µL Platelets 60,000/µL Which of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance of this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) Multifactorial. The diagnosis is systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). USMLE vignettes will often omit descriptors such as malar (butterfly) rash because they’re too easy. Arthritis is the most common presenting feature of SLE (>90%). Students should be aware of mucositis (mouth ulcers) and antibodies against hematologic cell lines as very high-yield in SLE. Antibodies are most frequently against platelets, resulting in isolated thrombocytopenia, but leuko- and erythropenia can also be seen. If there is an isolated erythropenia (i.e., no thrombocytopenia), then anemia of chronic disease should be suspected instead. Most autoimmune diseases (i.e., sarcoidosis, thyroiditis, pernicious anemia, etc.) do not carry a strict mode of inheritance and are best characterized as multifactorial – i.e, associated with many different gene and HLA combinations. This also applies to diabetes mellitus type I, androgenetic alopecia, pyloric stenosis, and cleft/lip palate

rapidFireQAs.q: A couple gives birth to a child with a cleft lip. Which of the following is the most likely probability they will have a second child with a cleft lip or palate?
rapidFireQAs.a: B) 2-4%. If a couple gives birth to a child with a cleft lip or palate, and neither parent has a cleft, the chance of a subsequent resulting in cleft lip or palate is approximately 2-4%. If one of the parents has a cleft lip or palate, the chance the child will have a cleft is closer to 5%. This same probability applies to congenital heart defects (i.e., ASD, VSD, etc.). The chance of recurrence is 2-4% (on NBME)
options: F) Same as general population since clefts are sporadic and multifactorial

rapidFireQAs.q: A two-week-old male vomits forcefully after feeds. The vomitus is non-bilious. Diagnosis is confirmed using abdominal ultrasound. Which of the following best describes this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) Multifactorial; one-off developmental anomaly. The highest yield genetics point about pyloric stenosis is that it is a one-off developmental anomaly – i.e., it is not part of a greater syndrome. This is in contrast to duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung, which are frequently associated with Down syndrome. This is asked on the NBMEs for Step 1. Pyloric stenosis is considered to be most often a multifactorial anomaly with no strict inheritance. Rarely, it may be considered to be autosomal dominant in some pedigrees, however this is not the primary mode of inheritance. Pyloric stenosis is best considered as part of a multifactorial inheritance. As discussed earlier, this is similar to cleft lip/palate and androgenetic alopecia, as well as autoimmune diseases such as diabetes mellitus type I, sarcoidosis, and SLE. Pyloric stenosis demonstrates a greater prevalence in first-born males, however it is not X-linked

rapidFireQAs.q: A 24-year-old woman (II-1 in the pedigree) has an autosomal recessive disorder. The frequency of the condition in the population is 1/40,000. What is the probability that II-3 and II-4 will have a son who is a carrier for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 1/600. Using Hardy-Weinberg: 1 = p2 + 2pq + q2 = p + q q2 = 1/40,000, therefore q = 1/200 and p = 199/200 ≈ 1. Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2 x 1 x 1/200 = 1/100 = chance II-4 is a carrier Since II-3 is a phenotypically normal sibling of a patient (II-1) with an autosomal recessive disease, the chance II-3 is a carrier is 2/3. Therefore, the chance II-3 and II-4 have a child who is a carrier for the disorder is 2/3 x 1/100 x 1/2 (since the Punnett square will have 2 x Aa) = 2/600 = 1/300 However, the question asks for the probability the couple will have a son who is a carrier, so we need to multiply this by the chance they have a son: 1/300 x 1/2 = 1/600

Therefore, the chance II-3 and II-4 have a child who is a carrier for the disorder is 2/3 x 1/100 x 1/2 (since the Punnett square will have 2 x Aa) = 2/600 = 1/300 However, the question asks for the probability the couple will have a son who is a carrier, so we need to multiply this by the chance they have a son: 1/300 x 1/2 = 1/600

rapidFireQAs.q: A healthy 25-year-old man has two siblings with cystic fibrosis. The carrier frequency in the general population is 1/25. Assuming no de novo mutations, what is the probability he will have a daughter who does not carry a cystic fibrosis mutation?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 1/300. The patient has siblings with cystic fibrosis. This means there is a 2/3 chance he is a carrier (i.e., he is healthy, so we can eliminate “aa” from his Punnett square, leaving 2x Aa and 1x AA as his possibilities). The carrier frequency in the general population is 1/25. So 2/3 x 1/25 x 1/4 (chance of having a child with AA in Punnett square; no disease allele) = 2/300 = 1/150. However, the question asks for the chance he will have a daughter who does not have a diseased allele, so we need to multiply by the chance he will have a daughter (1/2) So 1/150 x 1/2 = 1/300
