rapidFireQAs.q: In a clinical study of a disease, 225 people are examined for single nucleotide polymorphisms. The results are shown below. Genotype Number of people DD 60 DF 90 FF 75 If D is one allele and F is the other, which of the following is the frequency of allele D?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) 7/15. This question is “hard.” If each of the 225 people in the study have two alleles, then there are 450 total alleles. Solving for frequency of D allele: 60 people x (2D) = 120D alleles 90 people x (1D) = 90D alleles 120D + 90D = 210D 210D / 450 total alleles = 70/150 = 7/15 Solving for frequency of F allele: 75 people x (2F) = 150F 90 people x (1F) = 90F 150F + 90F = 240F 240F / 450 total alleles = 240/450 = 24/45 D = 210/450; F = 240/450, where 210/450 + 240/450 = 450/450 alleles total

rapidFireQAs.q: A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks’ gestation has an autosomal dominant disorder with 60% penetrance. A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) marker is identified on the diseased allele with a recombination fraction of 20%. Alleles A and B for this SNP marker are indicated on the pedigree. Which of the following is the probability the fetus will demonstrate disease phenotype?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 48%. The B marker in and of itself does not result in disease. It is localized geographically nearby to the disease mutation on the chromosome. Recombination occurs during prophase of meiosis-I, where chromatids crossover and exchange small amounts of genetic material, resulting in the unlinking of loci on the same chromatid Since there is a recombination fraction of 20%, there is a 20% chance the fetus received the B marker because it unlinked from the disease allele. This means there’s an 80% chance she still has the B marker linked to the disease allele, and thus carries the disease allele Since there this condition only bears 60% penetrance, the chance the fetus will demonstrate the disease phenotype is: 8/10 x 6/10 = 48/100 = 48%

rapidFireQAs.q: A 4-year-old girl has short stature. Both of her parents are of average stature. Genetic analysis shows paternal uniparental disomy of a particular locus. Which of the following mechanisms might explain the short stature?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) Paternal imprinting of two alleles. Maternal imprinting = gene coming from mom is silenced; requires receiving normal allele from dad in order to not have disease. Paternal imprinting = gene coming from dad is silenced; requires receiving normal allele from mom in order to not have disease. The girl has received both of her alleles from dad (i.e., paternal uniparental disomy) and has disease. This means both alleles are silenced coming from dad, which is the equivalent of having no allele at all. This concept is similar to Angelman and Prader-Willi syndrome, as discussed earlier Angelman syndrome = paternal imprinting + deleted/mutated allele from mom, OR paterna uniparental disomy (where both alleles can by all means be healthy but are silenced) Prader-Willi syndrome = maternal imprinting + deleted/mutated allele from dad, OR materna uniparental disomy (where both alleles can by all means be healthy but are silenced)
options: A) Maternal imprinting of one allele
B) Maternal imprinting of two alleles

rapidFireQAs.q: A 19-year-old man presents to the physician with abdominal pain, pink urine, and decreased sensation in his left hand. His symptoms are mitigated with administration of hematin Laboratory studies show deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. Which of the following inheritance patterns best describes this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Autosomal dominant. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant disorder of the heme synthesis pathway. It is caused by deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. The classic presentation is abdominal pain, red urine, and neuropathy. Symptomatology is improved with administration of hematin first-line; glucose may also be effective. Inheritance of AIP is asked on an offline NBME. Questions are known to repeat on the real USMLE, so this is worth knowing. Porphyria cutanea tarda, another heme synthesis disorder, is 20% of the time autosomal dominant and 80% of the time sporadic. This is due to deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Disease presentation is classically photosensitivity (blistering) and tea-colored urine

rapidFireQAs.q: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of fatigue. He recently recovered from a cold. Physical examination shows scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin: 10.4 g/dL Hematocrit: 31.2% MCV: 92 fL Direct antiglobulin test: Positive A blood smear is performed and shows spherocytes. Genetic testing is most likely to show which of the following?
rapidFireQAs.a: G) No specific mutation. Students freak out every time they see this question and think there’s an erratum Spherocytes can be seen in drug- and infection-induced hemolysis. They are not limited to hereditary spherocytosis. This is high-yield for USMLE. Hereditary spherocytosis is an autosomal dominant disorder most often in the ankyrin, spectrin, or band protein genes. Since it is AD, almost all individuals will only have one mutation (choice A). However, this patient has a positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test. This indicates there are antibodies against RBCs as the etiology for the hemolysis. In hereditary spherocytosis, there is a negative Coombs test because the disorder has nothing to do with antibodies; there is merely an RBC cytoskeletal defect due to mutation in ankyrin, spectrin, or band protein genes The positivity of the Coombs test indicates that a drug or infection has caused the hemolysis. The child recently had an upper respiratory tract infection. Viral etiology is a known precipitator of hemolysis, e.g., CMV

rapidFireQAs.q: A 27-year-old man presents to the physician because of a 3-month history of a bump on his skull. His father died of colon cancer at the age of 36. A radiograph of the patient’s skull and his colonoscopy are shown. Which of the following best describes this patient’s presentation?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Gardner syndrome; autosomal dominant. The patient has familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC gene) on chromosome 5 Gardner syndrome = FAP + soft tissue tumors (e.g., lipomas) or bone tumors (e.g., osteomas). The image shown is an osteoma of the skull. It is not a brain tumor Turcot syndrome = FAP + CNS tumors. The image shown is an osteoma of the skull. It is not a brain tumor. There is a 100% chance of development of colorectal cancer in FAP. Treatment is tota proctocolectomy at age 18, not repeated colonoscopies If the USMLE asks for the chance of this patient’s child going on to develop colon cancer, the answer is 50% – i.e., 50% chance of passing along the mutated APC gene x 100% chance of cancer FAP is characterized by hundreds to thousands of polyps observed on colonoscopy. In other words, there are “lots of polyps.” In contrast, Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) presents with “polyps but not as many as FAP.” FAP is notably described as innumerable polyps, as seen in the image. Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant. It is caused by mutations in mismatch repair genes (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2), resulting in microsatellite instability. Patients may also develop gynecologic cancers, or cancers of other organ systems (e.g., pancreas, duodenum) Peutz-Jegher is autosomal dominant and characterized by perioral melanosis (hyperpigmentation on the lips and around the mouth) and hamartomatous polyps. USMLE will show you a picture of hyperpigmentation of the lips and then the answer will just be “hamartomatous” for the polyp type
options: G) Turcot syndrome; autosomal dominant H) Turcot syndrome; autosomal recessive

rapidFireQAs.q: A couple has three children. Two of them have achondroplasia. Both parents are phenotypically normal. Which of the following best explains the disease pattern in this family?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Germline mosaicism. This is a favorite USMLE question. Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor gene, FGFR3. Most cases of achondroplasia occur, however, when both parents are phenotypically normal. This is because of germline (gonadal) mosaicism Germline (gonadal) mosaicism is when the spermatogonia or oogonia of one of the parents carry a mutation, but the somatic (body) cells do not. The result is that offspring can have an AD disorder despite the parents not being affected. Germline mosaicism is the answer classically for achondroplasia – i.e., the parents are normal but the child has the disease. The child will have 100% of his or her body cells affected because the original mutation was in the spermatogonia or oogonia of the parent, rather than occurring post-mitotically, as with somatic mosaicism. If the USMLE does not give achondroplasia, they will say two phenotypically normal parents have two children with an AD disorder, implying there is a germline mutation in one of the parents (usually the father). Incomplete penetrance is when not everyone with the diseased genotype bears the diseased phenotype (i.e., not everyone with the disease expresses it); this is sometimes referred to as “skipping a generation,” and also applies to the BRCA genes. Variable expressivity, in contrast, implies 100% penetrance – i.e., everyone with the disease expresses it in some form. The difference is the mere severity in which family members manifest the condition. NF1 is a classic example, where everyone with the disease has it, but whilst one family member might only present with axillary and groin freckling, another might develop pheochromocytoma and optic glioma. If the NBME/USMLE gives you a pedigree that looks like incomplete penetrance, but the diagnosis in the family is NF1, choose variable expressivity, not incomplete penetrance. A patient with minimal disease severity in NF1 might not report having it. Heteroplasmy is a phenomenon seen in mitochondrial disorders, an inheritance pattern characterized by strict maternal transmission (i.e., mothers transmit disease to sons and daughters; fathers never transmit disease), where varying amounts of diseased mitochondria are passed to the next generation, resulting in offspring with disease of varying severity. This is due to the mother’s oocytes carrying thousands of copies of mitochondrial DNA, where the oocytes differ in the ratios of diseased mitochondria they contain. Do not confuse this with variable expressivity, which instead refers to non-mitochondrial disorders, where a chromosomal mutation can result in varying severity of disease. Imprinting is when a gene is silenced coming from one parent. As mentioned earlier: Angelman syndrome = paternal imprinting + deleted/mutated allele from mom, OR paterna uniparental disomy (where both alleles can by all means be healthy but are silenced) Prader-Willi syndrome = maternal imprinting + deleted/mutated allele from dad, OR materna uniparental disomy (where both alleles can by all means be healthy but are silenced)

rapidFireQAs.q: A 16-year-old boy has two exons of his b-globin gene shown. 1 gggtacatcg gcctatatac ttatatattg atctagatcg aaacgaatcg 51 101 151 atctagatcg ttttatattg gcgtacatcg attCGAATCG ACCTGTATAG TGAGCGGATC CGatatattg Gcctatatac ataccgatcg ACTGGCGATA CGGTGTTTAC ccgtacattg aattacattc gcctttatcg atccagaccc Exons are given in bold capital letters. A mutation C→G at position 121 (red capital) is most likely to result in b-thalassemia due to which of the following mechanisms?
rapidFireQAs.a: A) Disruption of post-transcriptional processing. Letters that are bold and capitalized are exons. The patient therefore has a mutation within one of his intron sequences. Mutations within intron sequences are frequently splice-site mutations, resulting in impaired post- transcriptional processing. The USMLE might describe this type of mutation as “impairment of normal splicing by creation of new splice site.” Transcription = DNA → RNA Translation = RNA → protein When DNA is transcribed into RNA within the nucleus, the nascent RNA is known as heteronuclear RNA (hnRNA). It then undergoes three modifications within the nucleus: 1) Addition of 3’ poly-A tail 2) Addition of 5’ methylguanosine cap 3) Splicing out of introns After these three modifications occur within the nucleus, the hnRNA is now called mRNA. The mRNA then leaves the nucleus for the cytosol, where it is translated into protein. mRNA can also dock with P-bodies in the cytosol. These are storage sites for mRNA to be used later, or where additional modifications may occur. The splicing process occurs post-transcription, not post-translation. Do not confuse this process with the mechanism for Fragile X. As discussed earlier, an expansion of CGG >200 repeats within the 5’-untranslated region of the FMR1 gene results in hypermethylation and decreased transcription of the gene, not impaired splicing
options: B) Missense mutation resulting in misfolded protein
C) Nonsense mutation resulting in non-functional, truncated protein

rapidFireQAs.q: A 46-year-old man presents to the physician because of a painful big toe. Allopurinol has been ineffective in reducing recurrences. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern for this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) No specific enzyme deficiency or heritability. The image shows podagra (gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint) Some gene loci have been identified that have been posited to increase the risk of episodes, but gout is almost always an idiopathic condition not associated with any specific type of enzyme deficiency or inheritance pattern. High-yield risk factors include alcoholism and consumption of purine-rich foods such as anchovies and organ meats. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an XR condition leading to uric acid overproduction and gout. However this is a pediatric condition. The vignette will be a male infant who exhibits self-mutilation and has red-orange sandy urate crystals in his diaper
options: A) Autosomal dominant; complete penetrance; not syndromic
B) Autosomal dominant; incomplete penetrance; not syndromic

rapidFireQAs.q: A 23-year-old man presents to the physician because of a yellowish 1-cm growth over his left Achilles tendon. Laboratory studies show increased serum triglycerides and a milky appearance of the plasma following centrifugation. Enzyme analysis shows decreased activity of lipoprotein lipase. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern of this condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: B) Autosomal recessive. The diagnosis is familial hyperchylomicronemia, an autosomal recessive condition caused by deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or apolipoprotein C-II. Serum triglycerides and chylomicrons will be elevated. The serum bears a characteristic milky or creamy appearance upon centrifugation In contrast, familial hypercholesterolemia and familial hypertriglyceridemia are both autosomal dominant. Familial hypercholesterolemia causes an isolated increase in serum LDL. Heterozygosity will yield total cholesterol usually in the ~3-400s mg/dL. Homozygosity will yield ~700-1000 mg/dL. The mechanism is deficiency of LDL receptor (heterozygosity), or complete absence (homozygosity). Familial hypertriglyceridemia causes elevated serum triglycerides. The plasma is not described as milky or creamy upon centrifugation. The mechanism is increased hepatic production of VLDL

rapidFireQAs.explanation: The diagnosis is multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (MEN 1). The MEN syndromes are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. The patient has Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) resulting in duodenal ulcers The history of ureterolithiasis is secondary to hypercalcemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN 1: Pancreas, pituitary, parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia MEN1 gene; chromosome 11 MEN 2A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia RET GENE; chromosome 10 MEN 2B: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, Marfanoid body habitus, mucosal neuromas RET GENE; chromosome 10 Since MEN 1 is autosomal dominant, there is a 50% chance one of his daughters will have the condition. The question does not ask for the probability he will have a daughter with the condition (25%)

rapidFireQAs.q: A researcher wishes to investigate clonality of a population of leukemic cells. Analysis of which of the following would be best to determine monoclonality?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) X-chromosome-linked isoenzymes. Yes, this is a question. But it’s not our opinion that matters. It’s what shows up on the USMLE that does. Clonality refers to the source of certain cell types. For instance, most cancers are monoclonal, where they can ultimately be traced back to one cell that became neoplastic and then replicated. Polyclonal means a cell population is derived from many different cells. The most commonly used method for determining clonality is based on detection of X-chromosome sequence polymorphisms via identification of protein isoforms, methylation status, and transcribed mRNA. Bottom line: if you get a weird question about clonality, choose “X-chromosome-linked isoenzymes.”

rapidFireQAs.q: A 27-year-old man presents to the physician for a follow-up appointment. He has chronic kidney disease and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Previous enzyme analysis demonstrated a deficiency of a-galactosidase A. The patient’s torso is shown in the photograph below If the carrier frequency is 1/100,000, which of the following is the disease frequency in the population?
rapidFireQAs.a: D) 1 in 200,000. Fabry disease is an XR lysosomal storage disease due to deficiency of a-galactosidase A and accumulation of ceramide trihexoside. The classic presentation is a male with angiokeratomas (benign cutaneous capillary growths in the photograph) who has renal and/or cardiac pathology. This question is the reverse of Q16, where we solve for carrier frequency using disease frequency as a starting point. In question, we start with carrier frequency and solve for disease frequency. For XR disorders, disease frequency in males = q; disease frequency in females = q2 Since males cannot be carriers for XR disorders, carrier frequency in females = carrier frequency in the population. Using Hardy-Weinberg, carrier frequency = 2pq, where p + q = 1 Since 2pq = 1/100,000, and p ≈ 1, we have 2 x 1 x q = 1/100,000 = 2q; therefore q = 1/200,000. Had the question instead given us 1/200,000 as the disease frequency to start with, we would say: 2pq = 2 x 1 x 1/200,000 = 1/100,000 = carrier frequency. It should be noted that of the lysosomal storage diseases, Fabry and Hunter are both XR In contrast, Hurler, Gaucher, Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick, Krabbe, and metachromatic leukodystrophy are all AR. In addition, the glycogen storage diseases for USMLE are all AR

rapidFireQAs.q: An African American couple comes to the physician for preconception counseling. On a previous visit, the man had a hemoglobin electrophoresis performed that showed the presence of HbA. The woman has not yet been tested. If 1 out of 13 African Americans have sickle cell trait, what is the probability this couple will have a son who has sickle cell trait?
rapidFireQAs.a: E) 1/52. Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. The mutation is a glutamic acid → valine substitution on the b-globin gene. This results in more hydrophobic hemoglobin that is prone to sickling in states of dehydration and increased acidity. Two mutations results in sickle cell disease, where HbS, rather than HbA (normal adult hemoglobin), is seen on hemoglobin electrophoresis. One mutation results in sickle cell trait, where both HbA and HbS are seen on electrophoresis This man’s hemoglobin electrophoresis only demonstrated HbA, indicating he neither has the disease nor is a carrier. Since the carrier frequency in the African American population is 1 out of 13, the chance of this couple having a child with sickle cell trait is 1/13 x 1/2 = 1/26 Therefore, the chance of having a son with sickle cell trait is 1/26 x 1/2 (chance of having son) = 1/52. HY USMLE GENETICS
